#6262. Extreme weather in India and China shared a hidden atmospheric connection

A new analysis reveals how atmospheric circulation connected extreme heat in India with a rapid shift from flooding to humid heat in southern China.

India baked under a stubborn heat dome while southern China lurched from flooding into dangerous, humid heat.

A new analysis links the May 2026 extremes to the same sprawling high-pressure system.

Meng Gao from Hong Kong Baptist University led the analysis, with collaborators from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences and Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

For much of early May, temperatures across the Indian region studied had been below normal.

Starting on May 17, that changed sharply, with temperatures staying over 1°C above the recent May average.

The researchers combined weather observations, atmospheric reanalysis, and climate simulations to trace the change.

Their maps showed daily average temperatures exceeding 40°C in some locations.

May 20 stood out. Across the region studied, it was the hottest May 20 in the record stretching back to 1979.

Humidity added to the strain. The wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the combined effects of heat and moisture, ranked third-highest for that date.

For people working outside, particularly in northern India, the combination made an already difficult season more dangerous.

The developing El Niño offered part of the explanation. By May, the central and eastern equatorial Pacific had entered El Niño conditions.

Atmospheric circulation shifted far beyond its shores.

The researchers linked this developing El Niño to a stronger western Pacific subtropical high. This broad area of high pressure also stretched farther west than usual.

Meanwhile, a persistent wave pattern in the upper atmosphere strengthened another high-pressure system over the Iranian Plateau. That system moved eastward.

Over India, the two highs joined, creating a stable “heat dome.” Air sank beneath it, warming as it descended and helping keep skies clear.

With more sunshine reaching the ground, temperatures continued rising. Warm waters in the northern Indian Ocean also helped strengthen the Pacific high, further supporting the persistent heat.

In southern China, the same Pacific high helped produce a different sequence of hazards.

Guangdong had endured repeated downpours since early May.

Particularly heavy rain between May 19 and 23 brought widespread flooding, followed almost immediately by humid heat from May 24–29.

The abrupt switch followed the high-pressure system’s movement northwestward. Rain eased, sunshine increased, and descending air warmed the region.

The atmosphere, however, remained laden with moisture after the downpours. The result was a “rainfall-to-deadly humid heat” sequence, with little time between the two emergencies.

The paper reports dozens of heatstroke ambulance calls in Shenzhen and thousands of livestock deaths in Maoming.

Such dangerous combinations of heat and humidity arrived one to two months earlier than usual.

Air temperatures alone did not explain what happened in Guangdong. Readings were near the top of the historical range, but comparable heat had occurred before.

The difference was the moisture accompanying them. Relative humidity during the dangerous hours averaged about 60%, compared with roughly 50% during similarly hot hours in earlier years.

Humid air makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, limiting the body’s ability to shed heat. That means familiar thermometer readings can conceal much greater physical strain.

For several hours, conditions exceeded a modeled threshold for safe, sustained activity among healthy adults aged 65 or older. That applied even to sitting quietly or standing with minimal movement.

That threshold describes a particular group under specified conditions. Heat tolerance varies with age, activity, and exposure to sunlight.

The timing was exceptional too: these conditions appeared earlier than in any year of the available 2011–2025 comparison record.

The team also asked how human influence had changed the likelihood of India’s heat.

Using 11 climate models, the researchers compared simulations including human influences with a preindustrial climate.

Their central estimate suggested human influences had made a similarly intense Indian heatwave roughly 27 times more likely.

The estimated range was wide: about 16 to 52 times, at a 90% confidence level. The authors caution that differences between models and limitations in correcting their biases affect the result.

The authors describe the finding as evidence of a likely human contribution, with the precise scale still uncertain. The estimate applies to the Indian event, not to the entire sequence across both countries.

A common atmospheric influence helps explain why distant places suffered heat at nearly the same time. Whether those heatwaves also reinforced each other remains unresolved.

For southern China, the order of events matters. Flooding can damage electricity supplies and other infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable cooling when the heat follows.

Warnings therefore need to account for what happened in the preceding days.

A heat forecast issued during flood recovery may reach people whose homes, workplaces, and access to electricity are already disrupted.

The researchers call for stronger infrastructure and better preparation in vulnerable regions.

In places facing rapid weather reversals, flood response and heat preparation may need to happen at the same time.

The study is published in the journal Advances in Atmospheric Sciences.

One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature, researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo" group, the researchers wrote.

The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating, the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old.

To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different.

The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus, but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens, including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown.

The root system of the Chuanshandong tooth was complex and similar to what experts see in Homo erectus.

The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor, an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans.

The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution, researchers say.

Denisovans were first identified in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes, a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins.

The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor, two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus.

It's not clear whether they are our cousins.

It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins."

The Guangxi region of China is known for its caves, many of which have Pleistocene mammal fossils.

The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo'. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email.

Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus, then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave.

"I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers" that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses."

The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate.

"We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said.

Xing, S., Rao, H., Xie, G., Bai, F., Ge, J., Bennett, E.A., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Li, X., Viola, B., Sun, Q., Zhou, K., Li, Z., Jiangzuo, Q., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Feng, X., Lin, Q., Fu, Q. (2026). Middle-Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China. Nature. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11341-6

#6259. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#6258. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

Exceptionally high tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and abnormally warm water are converging on California's coast, with authorities urging residents to limit unnecessary travel this Thanksgiving.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Major flooding of up to 2.7 feet (0.8 meters) is expected in parts of California today (Nov. 25) as record-breaking tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and warmer-than-average ocean water converge along the state's coast.

The triple flooding threat is expected to hit the San Francisco Bay Area especially hard, with San Francisco International Airport and other low-lying areas of the city bracing for deluges, while officials warned of dangerous breaking waves measuring 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) tall along San Francisco's coast, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Meanwhile, in Southern California, coastal communities should expect potentially record-breaking "king tides" and breaking waves up to 15 feet (4.6 m) high, the National Weather Service warned on its website. King tides are exceptionally high tides that occur every year due to seasonal factors and the alignment of Earth, the sun and the moon — but this year's "super" El Niño has amplified the risk by pushing a massive "Kelvin wave" up California's coast.

Citing the forecast, several cities on California's central coast have closed beaches to shield people from hazards, including sudden waves that could wash beachgoers out to sea. Local authorities have also urged residents to limit unnecessary travel during the Thanksgiving holiday.

"As Californians head into the holiday, take a few minutes to check travel conditions, sign up for local emergency alerts, and make a plan to keep your family safe," California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday (Nov. 24).

The flooding comes as a perfect storm of adverse conditions has gathered on California's coastline. Scientists expected the king tides and the coastal flooding associated with them to emerge this time of the year. However, these powerful tides are now arriving on top of blistering sea temperatures due to accelerating climate change and the current El Niño event — the warm phase of a multiyear natural climate pattern that's in full swing and set to intensify through the end of the year.

Ocean water expands as it warms, swelling tides and raising the risk of strong surf and big waves. As a result, this year's tides are predicted to be at their highest levels since January 1983, when tides also coincided with El Niño-fueled storms, AFP reported.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Record-breaking “king tides,” combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to California during Thanksgiving week.

In January 1983, "all hell broke loose," Reinhard Flick, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, told AFP. "We had 13-foot (4-meter) waves offshore, the highest tides of the year, and hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It hit Northern California, Southern California, everybody."

Forecasts suggest this week's conditions won't be quite that bad. But there are risks to be aware of going into winter, especially as El Niño has yet to peak and more king tides are expected in December and January.

"It could potentially be quite bad if we also have rainfall and high waves at the same time during any one of these big events, especially December and January, when rainfall generally increases on our coast," Flick said.

Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't.

The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance, in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine, researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition.

When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down.

But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance. In one of the most severe forms, called Donohue syndrome, children can experience dangerously high blood sugar after eating, and unusually low blood sugar between meals, as well as poor growth. Most children with the condition die before their first birthday.

"Some [of these] patients produce extremely high levels of insulin, but their receptors cannot respond properly," study co-author Eunhee Choi, a cell biologist at Columbia University, told Live Science. "Simply giving more insulin may not solve the problem."

That's why Choi and her colleagues explored whether they could activate the receptor in another way.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In 2025, the researchers used computational tools, including AlphaFold2, an AI program that predicts protein structures and how they fit together, to develop proteins that activate insulin receptors in a different way than insulin does. In that previous study, one of those proteins, RF-409, lowered blood sugar in both healthy mice and mice with obesity. In the new research, the team wanted to see whether RF-409 could also activate defective insulin receptors.

First, they ran experiments with laboratory-grown mouse and rat cells and with healthy mice, both with working insulin receptors. This confirmed that RF-409 largely mimicked insulin's effects on cellular signaling and metabolism. In the mice, RF-409 had a nearly 60-fold longer half-life in the bloodstream than insulin, meaning the protein stays in circulation much longer before breaking down.

"Both these features make [the finding] more than just an elegant trick," said Dr. Rajiv Agarwal, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Unlike a protein that mimics only some of insulin's effects, RF-409 reproduces most of its normal signaling, "which matters in children who need growth as well as glucose control," he added.

Insulin (orange) plugs into the insulin receptor (blue) to change its shape and trigger signals inside cells. The new protein activates the receptor in a different way.

To test how RF-409 works with defective receptors, the researchers focused on a mutation previously identified in patients with Donohue syndrome; this genetic mutation alters a key part of the receptor's structure, preventing insulin from binding to it. Computer models suggested that RF-409 could bypass the affected region and hold the receptor in the shape needed to transmit signals inside cells.

The researchers genetically engineered mice to carry this mutation. Compared with mice that retained a functioning copy of the insulin receptor gene, these mice had, on average, roughly 2.5 times higher blood sugar and 10 times higher fasting insulin levels (the amount of insulin in blood after a period without food).

When injected with insulin, mice with defective receptors showed no substantial drop in blood sugar. Treatment with RF-409, however, lowered mice's blood sugar by roughly 60% within two hours.

"It is like designing a new key to open a defective lock," said Kalaiarasan Ponnusamy, a computational biologist at SRM Institute of Science and Technology in India who was not involved in the study. "From a computational protein-design perspective, this is a major advance because it demonstrates that entirely new proteins can be engineered to restore receptor function without correcting the underlying genetic mutation."

After 14 days of continuous treatment, five mice given RF-409 had lower blood sugar, maintained their body weight and retained more abdominal fat than five mice given a saline solution, for comparison. The treated mice also showed less pancreatic damage.

"Extending this approach to other disease-causing receptor mutations is a realistic possibility, provided the receptor retains its ability to transmit signals," Ponnusamy said. Some mutations, for instance, prevent insulin receptors from reaching the cell surface or transmitting signals inside cells at all. That means the technique demonstrated in the study is unlikely to work against such mutations.

Identifying which mutations can be treated in this way is now a priority for Choi. The team also plans to investigate how RF-409 affects different tissues in the body and whether it remains safe and effective over longer periods of treatment, she said.

Although Agarwal foresees several hurdles in bringing RF-409 into clinical use; for instance, the immune system's reaction to the protein will have to be carefully studied, and in general, it's challenging to run trials with infants with rare disorders. That said, he remains hopeful that it could help patients whose diseases have no treatments to treat the underlying cause.

"This is the first approach I have seen that addresses the actual defect rather than working around it," he said.

#6253. Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old question related to prime numbers

The Riemann hypothesis reveals a secret order hidden in the prime numbers.

ROBERT BROOK/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”

AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

#6251. The 6 Best Wood Stoves for Warmth, Ambiance, and More

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These simple appliances can generate an impressive amount of heat safely, and without increasing your energy bill.

The crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

Instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

More than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

The Expert (Alex Rennie): I'm a freelance writer who specializes in the Home Improvement, DIY, and Tool space. As a former residential and commercial carpenter, I use my hands-on experience to write practical buying guides, how-to articles, and product reviews. To choose my wood stove recommendations, I selected non-catalytic models that are affordable while still meeting EPA emissions standards. Among the wood stoves that made the cut, you’ll find a wide variety to meet your space limitations and style preferences while maintaining efficient BTU output.

One of the best things about having a huge fire in the middle of your home is that it lets you make the most of those rustic vibes. Many of the stoves I picked have a cooktop (very convenient) or a large window, so you can put your feet up and enjoy watching the flames. I also relied on prior research conducted by writer Alex Rennie, who also contributed to this article.

This pedestal stove from Ashley Hearth hits the sweet spot between size, heat output, and price. Its 2,500-square-foot heating range fits the average home with room to spare, and the brick-lined, 2.7-cubic-foot firebox accepts logs up to 21 inches long. That means fewer trips to the woodpile on cold nights.

One of the best features is the cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass, which helps keep soot off the window so you can enjoy the view of the fire. A non-catalytic secondary burn extracts more heat from every load and keeps emissions within EPA standards. It’s mobile-home approved when paired with the optional fresh air kit. The stove runs fine without electricity, but an optional blower will help push warm air into the rest of your house.

If you don’t need to heat your entire home, this compact Ashley Hearth model delivers plenty of warmth for the money. Its 68,000 BTU output covers up to 1,200 square feet. That makes it a smart fit for a cabin or an open living area, or as a supplemental heat source that takes some pressure off your furnace.

It shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. It also has a heavy cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass. It ships with both legs and a pedestal, so you can choose the look that suits your space. At 258 pounds, it’s relatively easy to move into place, and it’s mobile-home approved with the optional fresh air kit. The trade-off is a smaller 1.3-cubic-foot firebox, so you’ll load logs more often than with a larger stove.

If watching the fire matters more to you than heating every corner of the house, this Superior stove is built around the view. A large rectangular ceramic-glass door gives you a wide view of the flames, and the built-in air-wash system sweeps air across the glass to keep soot off.

The high-density firebrick holds heat longer for a more efficient burn. It puts out just 2.1 grams of particulate per hour, well under EPA limits. It fits logs up to 18 inches long, and one control handles the airflow. A black pedestal base comes standard, and an optional variable-speed blower can push warm air into nearby rooms.

The trade-off is a heating range of up to 1,400 square feet, so it’s best suited to a living room, a cabin, or a smaller home.

The WoodPro 300 is the largest model in the WoodPro line, built for anyone heating a large open floor plan, a farmhouse, or a drafty workshop. Its 2.26-cubic-foot firebox takes 18-inch logs and can burn for up to 12 hours on a single load, so you won’t have to refill it every couple of hours.

The stove is made of heavy-gauge steel with a cast-iron door. The Smart Air Control uses two levers, so the lighting procedure is simple: get the fire going, set the air, and leave it alone. It meets EPA 2020 standards at 1.6 grams of smoke per hour with 74.2 percent efficiency, and it’s approved for mobile homes with the outside air kit. Its peak output of 61,700 BTU is modest for a stove rated for 3,000 square feet, so treat that number as a best case in a well-insulated home, not something to count on in a cold climate.

This rustic model from Ashley Hearth—under the US Stove Company umbrella—the US1269E, is a natural fit for log cabin homes that want a rugged addition to their living space, or for anyone looking to add woodsy charm to their home.

My favorite feature is the oversized safety handle, which is comfortable to grab when opening or closing the door and stays cool to the touch, even when the stove is in operation.

Tested and certified to U.L.1482 by Warnock Hersey International, this stove’s 900-square-foot heating range isn’t the largest of my selections, but it's still impressive for its size. The integrated cooking surface on top is also a valuable feature.

If you’re looking for a pint-sized stove for a small space, including a mobile home, US Stove's Tiny Wood Stove may provide the perfect fit. The slim profile doesn’t mean it’s short on efficiency or on meeting emissions standards, and it still qualifies for the 30-percent Biomass federal tax credit.

A compact design, however, comes with a few caveats, including a rather small log size and a relatively low BTU output. Still, the US Stove Tiny Stove is a great trade-off for a single-room cabin or a more compact space in your home.

Wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

There are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is currently prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets

The size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you plan to stack and store firewood.

British Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

Decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

More isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

Modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

The size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially important if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

Generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all new wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

From insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

While cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

You can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

Yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you plan to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

Most new wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

A study claims that ancient "supervolcanoes" hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica. They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions.

About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive.

Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia.

"The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko, a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

"The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica."

Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet, so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history.

To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science.

They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales.

"We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said.

Alan Collins, an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email.

The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found.

Elias Rugen, a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said.

However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said.

An illustration of what the Pangea supercontinent would have looked like.

The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said.

"In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean."

Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit.

In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth.

Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion. The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans).

The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web.

However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing."

Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship."

However, the study did show that there was much more to discover under the ice in Antarctica.

"The most exciting aspect is the possibility that some of the largest mountain systems in Earth's history are effectively hidden beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet," Daczko said. "Antarctica potentially holds some of the most important remaining evidence for understanding the tectonic and environmental evolution of our planet."

#6249. Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Outwitting flying predators may have helped human ancestors evolve teamwork and language

Young olive baboons sit on the cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in Chad. New research suggests even adult baboons similar in size to some human ancestors are threatened by birds of prey.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

Biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as big cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” says Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter says.

“I found the evidence pretty compelling,” says Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

The eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter says.

The eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter says. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

The threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter says.

#6247. Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

In the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming new stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

But ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

In order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that shows what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Big Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations showed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

But to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies says, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

First, Davies’ team measured how many new stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how quickly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

The researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

The verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

Finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

Models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies says. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

The speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, says Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

Davies says that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies says. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really important for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

The case isn’t entirely closed. Davies says her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

Shreejaya Karantha is a science writer based in India. Her work has appeared in Sky & Telescope, Phys.org, Live Science US, and The Hindu.
