#6246. Vortex Crossfire vs. Leupold BX-3: Compact, Lightweight, Affordable Options That Offer More Than What Most Need

Both sit in the sweet spot of entry-level optics, but the Leupold shines for its low-light performance and center-image sharpness.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re spotting deer while on a hunt or identifying backyard birds, a trusty pair of 10x42 binoculars is a must-have for the outdoors. The 10x magnification isn’t too tight for closer quarters—think birdwatching—but gives you enough reach to spot animals 1,000 yards away, and it’s even sufficient for casual stargazing. The 42 mm objective lens (the one farther from your eyes) is wide enough to let in lots of light while keeping the field of vision natural.

Most people want a pair of binoculars that is decent, but not so exceptional that they have to spend thousands. I recommend the $150 to $300 range to get high-quality glass with coatings and enough performance that you won’t ever feel the need to upgrade.

Both the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 ($300) and the Leupold BX-3 ($230) fall right in this entry-level sweet spot. We tested both for our Best Binoculars buying guide and selected the Leupold BX-3 10x42 as our favorite binocular overall, but the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 performed very well, considering the price (often available for much less than retail, as it’s an older model than the Leupold, which debuted this year). As such, we compared the two head-to-head to identify meaningful differences. Here’s what we found.

I tested the Crossfire and BX-3 both handheld and tripod-mounted side-by-side in a range of conditions including sunset low-light environments, dense forest, long-distance expanses in the mountains, and several specialized setups designed to test things such as chromatic aberration, color fidelity, and image sharpness.

Truly objective stats about binocular performance can be hard to come by, so the somewhat arbitrary “tiers” of binoculars defined by price and place in a company’s lineup can serve as useful shorthand for how impressive the optical quality is.

Leupold’s BX-3 Alpine HD 10x42 binos are on the lower “budget” end of the company's numbered BX lineup that goes all the way up to the $3,999 BX-6 Range HD RangeFinder 10x42 binoculars. Still, I would argue that this tier of binocular at 10x42 offers you most of the performance of the high-end models. The higher you go in price, in my experience, the smaller the gains in clarity and performance

Vortex has many different lines, each one representing small jumps in features and optical quality. The Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 sits between its Triumph and Viper lines—the Triumph is our Best Budget and the Viper is Best for Hunting. The Crossfire HD 10x42 is entry-level in terms of price but is likely to be all the binoculars most people need, and still feels like a significant cost if binoculars are a nice-to-have item for you.

In terms of size and specs, the Leupold BX-3 10x42 is likely most comparable to the Vortex Viper HD 10x42, but at $749 MSRP doesn’t feel like an apples-to-apples comparison. The Viper HDs are great binoculars, especially for hunters who demand the dawn and dusk performance, but their price is more than double that of the BX-3 Alpine HD.

Note that both brands’ binos are usually available at retailers for much less than the MSRP on the official sites. At the time of this writing, the $230 Crossfire can be had in several places for $150 while the $299 BX-3 binos are consistently $199 at Scheel’s and Cabela’s, making the two models fairly close on real-world price.

Both brands market to the hunting community and it shows in these fairly similar designs. The roof prism design on both the BX-3 and Crossfire is near-standard in this type of binocular and it helps keep the size and weight down compared to bulkier designs used in the cheapest binos.

The Crossfire binos have a slightly flared look as you move from the eyepieces to the exit lenses while the Leupold are straighter, but the overall form factor is very similar. The Vortex Crossfire is slightly longer at 6 inches compared to the 5.7-inch Leupold BX-3.

Practically, these are both relatively compact, lightweight binos that will fit in most any aftermarket chest harness and won’t cause neck strain as quickly as bigger glass. The Crossfire is 0.4 ounces heavier than the BX—not really a meaningful difference in practice.

Both have hard plastic eyecups by default, which are more durable than the floppy rubber ones that often come on the cheapest binos. Leupold’s BX-3, however, comes with two other swappable eyecup options. During sunrise and sunset glassing, when low-angle sunlight constantly sneaks into your peripheral vision and nukes contrast, the alternate eyecups block the intrusions, making a legitimately noticeable difference.

This is the most important aspect of binoculars and also the hardest to objectively compare. Testing binoculars in person is always a smart idea if possible, as a few minutes scanning store shelves under artificial light isn't a great real-world test.

Both models provide decent center-image sharpness, especially considering their low cost. Moving closer to the edge of the image, clarity degrades in any binocular. The Leupold BX-3 binos have a slightly larger center area of sharpness than the Crossfire, perhaps 80 percent versus 70 percent.

A small but noticeable difference that subtly adds to the comfort of using them and gives Leupold an edge. In real-world use spotting animals such as bighorn sheep at long distances, I didn’t even notice. Like many marginal improvements you get with better binos, the sharper image just adds subtly to the overall picture clarity. For hunters, it’s unlikely to be the difference between success and failure, but it may make long sessions a touch easier and more enjoyable.

I expected much more noticeable color fringing with the Crossfire HD, but it wasn’t pronounced in either pair. This defect in imagery in binocular views and photography occurs when light gets distorted and unnatural colors appear, usually around the edges of objects such as dark hair on an animal appearing blue or purple.

Both the Crossfire and BX-3 have HD in the name, which most likely refers to the glass elements and coating that help reduce glare, fringing, and generally produce a sharper image. For the most part, I noticed few differences in object sharpness and color. Both binos produce refreshingly neutral, natural colors in a range of light conditions.

Glare was less pronounced in the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD than the Vortex Crossfire HD. Neither was able to eliminate glare entirely in challenging conditions such as pointing roughly 20 degrees off from the sun near sunset. But the portion of the view obscured by glare was smaller in the BX-3. It was also less hazy and diffuse, which left the portion of the view not obscured by glare clearer. This is, again, not a massive difference but adds incrementally to a slightly better optical quality overall for the BX-3.

Dusk, dawn, and dark forests are an extreme that can expose cheaper binoculars. For hunters, the crepuscular hours are when animals are usually most active—and when they’re hardest to pick out through your optics. Birdwatchers and casual users will be less affected if a bino struggles to gather dwindling light, but performance in these conditions is a reasonable indicator of overall optical quality.

The Leupold BX-3 was noticeably better in the worst, last-minute-of-the-day conditions, but the differences were only pronounced at the extremes. The brighter image wasn’t noticeable until well into the “blue hour” that comes before sunrise and after sunset. This makes using brighter optics much easier for hunters desperately scanning dwindling light but might not sway more casual users. The brightness of the two pairs was mostly indistinguishable in midday sun.

These are fairly closely matched binoculars, though the Leupold was the better pair whenever there was an edge to be had. The most meaningful separators were low-light brightness and center-image sharpness.

I didn’t find this surprising as the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD costs more, and the Vortex Crossfire HD is more of an entry-level option that sits maybe one level below the BX-3 in the loose optical hierarchy of grades of binoculars. Rather than an apples-to-oranges comparison, testing these side-by-side served as a reminder of how subtle the improvements are between tiers and price jumps in the binocular world.

While dedicated hunters and birders might be willing to pay $50 to $100 more for the jump in quality to the BX-3, the affordability of the Crossfire HD will appeal to those who don’t need 10 percent better. Either pair presents a good value in their respective categories, but you’ll have to decide which you value more—a lower price or better performance in challenging conditions.

#6245. Phaethon’s fiery folly

Even the best-laid plans can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” says Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Euclid space telescope image of the newfound quasar (red dot in the center), which is further away than any known active galactic nucleus found yet.

Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe.

"Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement. "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both."

The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics.

A quasar, short for "quasi-stellar radio source," is an incredibly bright core at the center of some galaxies — a region known as the active galactic nucleus (AGN). They form when supermassive black holes, which lurk at the hearts of most galaxies, start to binge on nearby matter. Once enough swirling material accumulates around these black holes, it heats up and glows intensely before falling into the object. What sets quasars apart from other AGNs is their sheer luminosity; they can be brighter than all the stars in a galaxy combined.

Quasars were much more common early in the universe than they are today. They are thought to have peaked in number about 10 billion years ago. Observing them can give scientists important clues as to how galaxies evolve — and how their supermassive black holes develop.

The quasar was discovered during the Euclid Wide Survey's scan of the sky — marked here in light yellow. Dark yellow patches show the target areas of Euclid's Deep Survey, which will repeatedly view smaller parts of the sky.

Because it takes time for light to travel, observing celestial objects that are very far away is tantamount to peering back in time. We see galaxies very near to Earth as they were only a few thousand years ago; conversely, we see galaxies very far away from us as they were billions of years ago, because their light is only now reaching our telescopes. The older the galaxy, the more red its light becomes as it stretches across the universe — a phenomenon called "redshift."

Using data from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Space Agency's Euclid Wide Survey, the researchers behind the new study identified a quasar with a redshift of 8.13 — the first such object ever found with a redshift beyond 8. This makes it the oldest quasar yet observed, at approximately 13.1 billion years old. For reference, the universe itself is thought to be 13.8 billion years old.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The scientists named the object Dún Aonghasa, after a prehistoric cliff fort on the Atlantic-facing edge of Inis Mór, an island off the coast of Ireland. The name is meant to reflect the quasar's position at the very edge of our current observational frontier for the cosmos.

According to the researchers, Dún Aonghasa also appears to be growing more slowly than astronomers previously thought possible, given its size. This suggests that its supermassive black hole may have gone through a massive growth spurt, followed by a period of much slower growth in the distant past. The discovery could put new constraints on black hole growth models, which are already being challenged by previous JWST detections of supermassive monsters that seem to have grown too big for their early place in cosmic history.

Future observations from Euclid and JWST could help researchers test this hypothesis and see if it holds for other ancient quasars, the researchers said.

#6242. The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 25: Uranus at opposition

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

#6241. This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By sharing his rare condition, he’s helping scientists study how brains perceive faces

A brain surgery left a man with a big change in how faces appear. Sometimes, his cat’s eyes appear on a family member’s face, and vice versa. He and scientists worked with generative AI tools to create this image of his perception.

AI-generated images co-created by Brad Duchaine and Karl

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was currently looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

It was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December issue of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a new context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

The researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”

Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”

Duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine says. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

“What is new about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” says Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”

During a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine says. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case shows some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

“It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl says, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in new spots.

Using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom says. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”

#6240. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6239. Nov. 25, 1783: The birth of Claude-Louis Mathieu

Born in Macon, France, on Nov. 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu showed an aptitude for mathematics from a young age. Despite his family’s poverty and his father’s wish for him to be a carpenter, Mathieu moved to Paris in 1801 to study for admission to the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique. He became a student at Ecole Polytechnique two years later and graduated from the school in 1805.

A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances. He also became a professor of astronomy at the College de France, a writer and editor, and a driving force behind the adoption of the metric system in France. Mathieu was elected president of the International Metre Commission in 1870 although he was in his late 80s, and continued to work in that position into his 90s.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6238. The 8 Best Smokers to Cook Low and Slow

From wood pellets to charcoal, these cookers use a little heat and a lot of time to make incredible barbecue.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The best smokers help you achieve the sweet and savory flavor combinations that make smoked meat so tasty. Whether pulled pork, brisket, ribs, or chicken is on the menu, this type of specialized home grill brings a new dimension to your backyard barbecues all year long.

There isn’t just one type of smoker. Purists prefer the iconic offset or “barrel” smoker, which reflects an array of regional barbecue traditions found in Texas, Memphis, Kansas City, and the Carolinas. In the last decade or so, increased interest in the art of barbecue has led to an expanded range of more beginner-friendly alternatives, including hardwood charcoal smokers and low-maintenance wood pellet smokers.

Some models have made the cooking process even easier with WiFi-enabled smart features for monitoring and adjusting internal temperature via an app on your phone. That way, you don’t have to stand by for hours as you cook.

If you’re in the market for a new smoker, we have one for every setup and skill level. Continue reading for our choices of the best smokers and tips on what to consider before you buy.

We’ve tested dozens of grills and smokers of all different shapes and sizes over the years. Tony Carrick, coauthor of this article, currently uses a Masterbuilt charcoal-fed gravity smoker and a Weber Smokey Joe at home. David Dritsas is a reviews editor at Popular Mechanics and is an amateur cook who has tested a variety of grills. Both drew on their combined experience with smokers, along with external research, to inform our recommendations.

We supplemented our own experience and criteria for smokers with extensive research into the various types that are available. We compared specifications of dozens of smokers and consulted user reviews to find trends or qualities that stand out (both positively and negatively) and might impact your ultimate choice. Our final recommendations span a range of designs and price points, and each offers solid performance, durable build quality, and great value.

One of the first things you notice about the Pit Boss Navigator 1600M is how well-constructed it is. The metal frame is sturdy, the hardware is strong, and the main section is well-insulated, including a heavy hood that is lined all the way around the edges by a fireproof, padded seal that keeps the heat in. (The Navigator performed very well in that regard.)

It has a large hopper that holds up to 30 pounds of pellets, and the controls are easy to understand. There’s WiFi on board, and we experienced a one-time issue where the app disconnected and would not reconnect, but it otherwise worked well, and navigation was intuitive. The Navigator also has two wired thermometer probes, for which you can set temperature alerts, so you know when your meats are ready.

For our main cooking test, we smoked a flat iron steak, as well as a mix of garlic-marinated zucchini, onions, and red peppers (that was enclosed in aluminum foil, open at the top). We were impressed with how quickly the grill heated up and how efficiently it maintained the temperature (even as we grilled in cold weather).

The only feature we did not find exceptional was the flame broil setting, which allows you to expose food to the flames of the burner cup directly. While it technically works, the cooking area of this feature is only roughly 3 inches in diameter, so it’s not very effective for large pieces of meat or more than one burger. But that complaint is a minor one.

You don’t have to spend a lot of money to get proficient at smoking food, and Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe proves that point. It’s a very basic charcoal barrel-shaped model that requires you to stay near and mind the coals to maintain the temperature, but it offers a few nice extra features to help you do it.

The biggest is the three-position charcoal tray. Set it high to sear meat while grilling or set it low to help keep temperatures down around 250 degrees Fahrenheit when smoking low and slow. Of course, airflow is integral to smoking, and there are three control options here, including a side vent, a chimney, and a large front door that you can also open to gain access to the coals for adjustment without having to remove the cooking grates. We used it several times to spread out the charcoal when things were getting a bit too hot.

There’s also a built-in thermometer that’s easy to read, even from a short distance, two side tables, and a lower shelf. All said and done, even if you don’t use it as a smoker, we think this makes for a fantastic charcoal grill with plenty of cooking area (940 square inches) to make a ton of burgers for your next barbecue party.

The Laredo Deluxe is not as solidly constructed as some of the other selections on our list, but that’s to be expected for a grill that’s usually on sale for under $300. We smoked a delicious brisket with ease during our tests, and we’d happily do so again.

Full Oklahoma Joe’s Laredo Deluxe Grill and Smoker Review

Masterbuilt’s Gravity Series 800 gives you unique flavor from hardwood charcoal smoke in your barbecue without dealing with all the fuss of micromanaging your smoker. It pairs a large gravity-fed hopper for hardwood charcoal with a digital thermostat that controls the internal temperature. The hopper keeps your cooking fire fed, while an internal fan system regulates temperature to maintain consistency. Just load it up, light it, and let it cook for hours with minimal maintenance.

As with our top pick, the Gravity Series 800 features wireless-enabled smart controls, which allow you to monitor the temperature from your phone. It also includes a digital meat probe.

With 800 square inches of cooking surface, you’re getting a lot of space here. There’s plenty of room for ribs, whole chickens, and pork butts. But at nearly five feet wide, the Masterbuilt 800 is a big boy—possibly too big for some decks and patios. That said, it also functions as a standard charcoal grill and a flat-top griddle, so you could ditch your standard grill to make space for it.

This Woodridge Pro is a midrange model in Traeger’s line of pellet smokers, featuring some of the technology found in its higher-end models but at a lower price. When we unboxed the grill, we were impressed by how easy it was to put together, despite the large number of loose parts. Traeger’s assembly guide was one of the best we’ve seen, with clear directions and marked boxes with icons that corresponded to the instructions.

Some construction elements, such as light plastic wheels and thin grill grates, seemed lacking, and there’s no seal around the interior of the hood (which helps with heat retention). Once together, however, this grill is sturdy and not at all difficult to move around. We really appreciate that the top of the pellet hopper serves as an extra shelf, which is handy and something you don’t always get with other grills. There’s also a special pellet sensor that lets you know if pellets are running low.

The Woodridge Pro is extremely straightforward to operate. The rather retro display with large block numbers is readable from a distance, and basic temperature control is quick to adjust and set with a large push-button dial. You can also set a timer, check probe temperature, and with the press of a button, add extra smoky flavor for slow cooks under 225 degrees Fahrenheit. One thing we really liked was a motion graphic that shows whether the grill is heating up or lowering the temperature. During our tests, it was helpful to have that feature as a reminder as we multitasked. Wireless control is available with WiFi and Bluetooth, and the app, named WiFire, is easy to use.

The food we made turned out delicious, whether slow-cooked for a deeper smoky flavor or grilled at a higher temperature for just a hint. We used both the included wired probe to monitor temperature, as well as a Meater thermometer, and found some slight discrepancies between the grill’s temperature setting and the ambient temperature on the Meater. We found ourselves pushing the temperature up a few degrees to get it where we wanted it to be. This didn’t mar the experience too greatly, however. The Woodridge Pro is a reliable pellet grill that’s fun to use and a worthy addition to any back patio.

In many ways, the 18-Inch Smokey Mountain from Weber is a standard water smoker (a 14-inch model is also available). Like similar models, it has a bottom rack and retaining ring for the charcoal, a large bowl for water, and two racks for smoking food. But it stands out because it’s made from heavier porcelain-enameled steel, which helps retain heat and maintain a consistent temperature, as well as a heat shield on the bottom to protect your deck or lawn. It also comes with a cover.

When we first fired it up to season the smoker, we took the opportunity to get familiar with how to use the three air vents around the bottom, as well as the top vent, to help hold a desired temperature. To help you gauge this, there’s a thermometer in the lid that shows a highlighted smoking zone from 200 to 275 degrees Fahrenheit, and we found it was relatively easy to keep it in that range.

We put this to the real-world test when smoking some beef jerky. To do this, we wanted to keep the temperature on the lower side at around 200 degrees Fahrenheit. This proved a little challenging; the temperature kept creeping up, so we watched it closely and adjusted the vents as needed. In the end, the jerky smoked a bit faster than we intended. In hindsight, we used a little too much charcoal, which generated more heat than we needed. While this was our mistake, it shows just how well this smoker can retain heat.

When smoking a smaller-sized brisket, we more successfully managed the temperature and were able to hold close to 225 degrees Fahrenheit for the 5 hours it took to smoke it. One thing we really appreciated during longer smoking sessions was the large door, which made it easy to add fuel and wood chips. The Smokey Mountain is a basic smoker that will require a little experience to use effectively, but will ultimately be worth the time and produce great results. — tested by Bradley Ford

Though they are frowned upon by traditionalists, electric smokers like this one from East Oak are the quickest way for new barbecuers to enter the world of smoking. Its digital controls make it easy to maintain specific temperatures, and the combination of a side wood chip loader and glass door means you can check on your cook without opening the door, which could impact your cooking temperature.

The 725-square-inch cooking surface gives you plenty of room to experiment with various types of food in a single session, but the smoker itself is quite slim, measuring nearly 19 inches wide and 18 inches deep, so it won’t take up a lot of space on your deck or patio. Bottom line: This is a straightforward and, above all, convenient way to try smoking barbecue at home.

If a grill could be a pop-culture icon, the Big Green Egg is it. The brand has a whole group of fans—known as Eggheads—who gather at grilling events called EGGfests held all across the country. And it’s not just home enthusiasts. According to the company, nearly 1,800 restaurants use this extremely popular kamado grill. Its excellent heat retention and temperature range, enabled by its shape and porcelain-coated ceramic enclosures, make them an instant upgrade over your average gas or charcoal grill.

That thick ceramic body is also very effective at retaining heat, making it very effective for cooking low and slow. Just add some smoking wood, and you can smoke a brisket overnight. This grill can get as hot as 750 degrees Fahrenheit when you’re grilling, but smokers will want to maintain a stable 225 to 300 degrees using the air vents at the top and the bottom of the egg. And it’s large enough to feed a crowd—we’re talking about smoking a 20-pound turkey for Thanksgiving.

This small electric smoker from GE lets you take your smoking indoors. It uses two heat sources—one to cook food and the other to burn pellets—along with a filtration device to prevent the smoke from filling your kitchen. Its modest 293 square inches of cooking surface is enough to smoke three half racks of ribs or a small pork butt.

There’s a bevy of controls for setting smoke levels and adjusting temperatures. There are also preset food settings, including brisket, ribs, pork butt, and chicken wings. Built-in probes and WiFi connectivity let you monitor meat temperatures remotely, and this smoker is compatible with voice controls via Amazon Alexa and Google Home.

Traditional offset or “barrel” smokers feature two parts: A large main cooking chamber for your food and a smaller cook box for the fuel. The wood or charcoal burns, heating the main chamber and filling it with smoke, which slowly cooks the meat with indirect heat and infuses it with smoky flavor. Offset smokers, like the Royal Gourmet model we recommend as our Best Value pick, are beloved by barbecue aficionados, but are also the most challenging to use. Learning how to control the temperature in an offset smoker takes practice.

Vertical or “cabinet” smokers have a tall, closet-like design with a single door on the front and three to five racks for food inside. The heat source sits in the base, allowing the heat and smoke to waft upward and fill the space. Going high instead of wide makes a vertical smoker more compact, so it’s a good option if you don’t have much room on your patio. That said, the narrow profile may limit your ability to cook large pieces of meat, such as a full rack of ribs.

Like vertical smokers, the pill-shaped bullet smoker has a fuel area at the bottom with the main cooking chamber above. Vents on the bottom and top of the smoker allow you to control the temperature inside the chamber, and a water pan sits just below the cook area to keep food moist. Bullet smokers are compact, however, and some models are stacked so tightly that you may have trouble accessing the food on the middle racks mid-cook.

Most pellet smokers, including the Traeger Ironwood 885, look more like a grill than a smoker, with a wide cook box and a clamshell lid that opens up to reveal a broad cooking surface. To generate smoke and heat, an electric auger feeds small hardwood pellets from a hopper on the back or side into a fire inside the cook box. The auger automatically adds fuel to the fire based on the temperature you dial in on the smoker’s digital thermostat, so you don’t need to babysit the smoker to maintain the proper temperature. However, they require a power source and tend to be the most expensive.

Kamado grills, like the famous Big Green Egg, are hybrid grill-smokers. These large, acorn-shaped ceramic cook boxes can maintain low temperatures for many hours or build up scorching heat with temperatures that eclipse 800 degrees. It’s an incredibly versatile option, which has made it a gateway device for new barbecuers.

Smokers can use a variety of fuel types, including hardwood, charcoal, gas, electricity, or wood pellets. Hardwood and charcoal are the fuels of choice for smoking purists. This combination creates a lot of smoke, maximizing that flavor. Maintaining a consistent low temperature takes time to learn, though, and it makes more of a mess with leftover ash.

Electric and gas smokers are convenient because they require little to no maintenance, but they don’t inherently produce smoke. Instead, they rely on wood chip trays that aren’t as effective as wood, charcoal, or pellets at instilling flavor into food. However, they still can produce decent results.

Pellet smokers use compressed wood pellets that generate real smoke for instilling flavor into food, while minimizing maintenance with automatic temperature regulation. Pellet grills offer excellent heat retention and temperature control, but don’t need as much constant attention as charcoal or wood grills.

Smoking meat can take eight hours or more, depending on the cut, so you’ll probably want to cook as much as you can in one session. It’s important to look for a smoker with an efficient interior design that has space for everything you want to cook. The average cooking surface size for a smoker is around 550 square inches, which is enough to fit five full racks of ribs, four whole chickens, or five pork butts. That said, I’ve seen cooking surfaces range in size from 250 square inches to more than 800.

Some modern smokers can connect to your smartphone via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, allowing you to track their internal temperature, change temperature settings, and monitor meat probes remotely through an app. They can also send you alerts if the smoker’s internal temperature rises or falls, the food reaches a target temperature, or if it’s low on fuel, allowing you to keep tabs on your smoker without having to hover over it.

What’s the best temperature for smoking meat?

With a smoker, you want to keep the temperature low and cook for a long time. Depending on what you’re cooking, I’d recommend maintaining your heat between 190 and 225 degrees. In that range, you will cook your meat slowly enough to make it incredibly tender and infuse it with smoky flavor.

It depends on what you’re cooking. Smoking a rack of ribs typically takes between four and five hours, but a pork butt may need 8 to 10 hours. Brisket is well-known for needing an especially long smoke—around 12 to 18 hours.

Technically, yes. You can add a smoker box to a gas grill, which holds wood chips to generate smoke. So long as you keep the top of the grill closed, that’s a smoker. Make sure to set up the grill so that the food is not sitting directly above the heat source, and set the burners so that the grill only heats to a maximum of 225 degrees with the lid closed.

That said, it’s far from ideal. It’s more difficult to maintain the consistently low temperatures needed for smoking with a gas grill than it is with a dedicated smoker. On top of that, flames from a gas grill will not impart the same distinctive taste as a proper smoker burning charcoal or hardwood. (Purists don’t even like gas as a fuel for dedicated smokers.)

Researchers knew that cholesterol and blood pressure are important for estimating stroke risk, but a new study suggests these should be measured far earlier in life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Cardiovascular disease has long been linked to risk factors like high blood pressure and cholesterol — but a new study suggests that these factors, combined with proteins in the blood, could help forecast people's risk of heart attack and stroke decades in advance.

The new study, published Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal JAMA Network Open, took a broad view of the factors that spike the risk of stroke or heart attack. The researchers found that warning signs for these conditions can be seen in patients' health data up to 30 years before they happen.

The researchers say their work shows that some understudied biomarkers — measurable signals in the blood — could be useful tools in anticipating later conditions.

"We did know that there are some well-established risk factors that are related to heart disease, for example, blood pressure, cholesterol," said study co-author Dorien Kimenai, an epidemiologist at the University of Edinburgh. But "nobody really has looked at the patterns of these risk factors prior to when these people are getting cardiovascular events — not systematically."

For the new study, the scientists tracked data patterns from a diverse group of nearly 114,000 healthy people over 34 years. Their data spanned four long-term health studies conducted in the U.S., U.K., and Norway. At the end of the study period, the researchers divided data from participants who were still healthy at that juncture from those who had experienced heart attacks or strokes and either died or survived the events.

But even at the study's outset, these two groups' blood pressure and cholesterol data showed a clear divergence.

"We did see that, even three decades before, already, that these patterns were different," said Kimenai. That suggests, she added, that the difference between the two groups likely began even earlier than that.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also divided their participants by sex and age, finding that men and women experienced different trajectories in their cardiovascular disease risk over time. Women, on average, started with lower blood pressure than men in middle age, but that switched later in life.

"It shows that the age effect is as important as the sex differences," Kimenai said. In short, both factors need to be taken into account.

Dr. Sintip Pattanakuhar, a clinician scientist at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland who was not involved in the study, said that while these risk factors can't be modified in the way blood pressure or cholesterol can, age and sex could be incorporated into personalized screening programs for cardiovascular risk.

During a stroke, the brain's blood supply is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds inside the organ. This reduces the blood and oxygen supply in certain parts of the brain, driving tissue damage and death.

The team also looked at the trajectories of biomarker proteins that circulate in the bloodstream and are linked to cardiovascular disease. These include cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are released by damaged heart muscle tissue and used to diagnose a heart attack. They also included C-reactive protein, a liver-borne molecule that signals rising inflammation in the body.

Differences in cardiac troponin and C-reactive protein were visible in people who would go on to have a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before they happened. For NT-proBNP, the differences emerged about 10 years before.

That said, Kimenai cautioned that the biomarker data came from fewer participants than the full study cohort, so these results bear further confirmation.

Dr. Deepak Bhatt, director of the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, said the study's blood pressure and cholesterol data confirmed what cardiologists had long suspected about these risk factors: that these modifiable factors predict cardiovascular disease. Bhatt, who was not involved in the study, added that the biomarker data in this study built on other studies that have also shown that cardiovascular events can be predicted years before they happen.

"What this adds is that it's actually predicting events decades before," he said.

The study's clearest message was that people should get their cardiovascular risk factors checked early, Kimenai said.

"When you're 40 years old, get your risk assessments and your blood pressure measured," she said. "Because these are the things you can change. If you've then been identified as having hypertension, then you can get those drugs that are very effective and safe and efficient to alter the pattern."

However, while the value of checking blood pressure and cholesterol is well established, Kimenai and Bhatt agreed that the clinical value of the biomarker data was less clear at this stage. Bhatt said that he might advise a patient with high blood pressure to start medication and cut out salt, for example, but the way forward for someone with an elevated biomarker reading is less clear for now.

"Ideally, more work will be done" to see whether panels of biomarkers, perhaps combined with tools that measure genetic risk, could flag patients at very high risk of having heart attacks and strokes and should be treated differently than a patient with lower risk, Bhatt suggested. "That's sort of the missing piece of the Holy Grail of prevention."

#6235. Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amber fossils preserve tiny paddles on the lower leg that could have powered each stroke

Ancient grasshoppers with spindly legs glide across water in this illustration, similar to how they may have scooted nearly 100 million years ago.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.

Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.“I was genuinely amazed,” says Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”

Under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.

The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the new family Hydrelcanidae.

“Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu says. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.

The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.

And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team says.

#6234. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6233. The 8 Best Portable Refrigerators If You’re Tired of Buying Bags of Ice

This convenient appliance works better than your average cooler and offers versatile power options. Here are the ones we recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Even the best coolers we’ve tested from names like Yeti, Coleman, and RTIC with superior insulation eventually get too warm for ice to stay frozen. That’s where portable refrigerators shine, offering cooling capability that you just can’t get from a regular cooler. They’re great for long camping trips where you need to keep meat and other food at safe temperatures and come in plenty of sizes to suit hardcore camper rigs and RVs or fit in a standard sedan.

Portable refrigerators—often called car refrigerators—plug into your car’s 12-volt outlet, an AC outlet, or a portable power station. They’re pricier and heavier than the standard cooler, but they're more efficient at cooling. And you get to skip the expense and hassle of dealing with bags of ice. They can also be helpful around the house if your fridge breaks or there’s a power outage.

We used our expertise on coolers, power stations, and camping gear to find the best portable refrigerators. We checked camping and overlanding gear reviews and forums to find models that hold up on long treks in remote areas and are viable alternatives for people who don't want to deal with bags of ice for a cooler.

We chose options in different capacities and across a range of prices and prioritized models that offer convenient features like USB chargers, wheels, and LED lights. If you want some extra cooling power on-the-go, consider one of the portable refrigerators for your next trek.

This portable fridge from Bodega has great build quality, convenient features for easy portability, and cools down fast. The compressor can cool the interior down to 32 degrees Fahrenheit in about 30 minutes.

It has two separate compartments to keep things organized. They can’t be individually controlled but the smaller section typically gets cooler than the larger side. It also has a user-friendly app for setting the temperature and a USB port to charge other devices. Some customers report minor differences between the temperature they see on the app versus the actual internal temperature, but say it’s only off by a couple degrees.

The portable refrigerator has sturdy handles and a built-in LED light so you can quickly find what you need in the dark. Standout features include wheels and a drain plug—two things that are standard on most larger coolers but something a lot of portable fridges lack. The lid can be opened from either side or popped off entirely for fast loading.

This portable refrigerator is a great value for efficient cooling, a low power draw, and large capacity. The 59-quart space is split into two zones for easy organizing and the unit comes with a removable wire basket.

Its tall, slender shape fits easily behind a row of seats in the car. The handles are also removable to make for easy stowing. The app lets you set and monitor temps, though you can’t do much else. Some users report the app is user-friendly but wish it had more features.

The Alpicool is a budget portable refrigerator that cools down fast to roughly zero degrees Fahrenheit and operates quietly in comparison to most other models.

It has an automatic shutoff to ensure it doesn’t drain your car or portable battery and eco mode that pulls less energy. An external LCD display and control panel shows you the interior temperature. This budget option also has an LED light inside and a drain plug.

Setup is rather easy but the included manual doesn’t show you how to convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit. The brand’s website has a detailed owner’s manual that's more helpful.

Thinking of Igloo might still conjure the image of the old-school Playmate cooler you had as a kid. But the ICF electric cooler is anything but that. The portable refrigerator has a sturdy plastic build that can handle the bumps and bruises that come with transporting it to sporting events, grocery stores, and campgrounds.

Its spacious interior works as one large storage space or, with the help of the included removable divider, two separate areas. This helps separate dry items like canned drinks from wet items like fruit and sandwiches. The ICF is also remarkably simple. All the controls are built right onto the body, so all you have to do is turn it on and set the temperature.

Like other portable refrigerators, the ICF has a three-stage battery protection system to prevent it from draining your car battery.

The Bouge comes in a compact package that can serve as a personal cooler for a remote overnight, or extra storage on long treks. It has a single compartment that works as a fridge or freezer.

Set the temperature from the external control panel and monitor through the LCD thermometer. There’s no app to keep tabs on the temperature while driving but customers report it stays consistent even in hotter ambient temps. Recessed handles add to its space-saving design.

Some reviews mention the external thermometer can be off as much as seven degrees—a bit higher than most other models.

The Travoca Rigel eCooler has a number of small, but notable, features that intrigued us right away. For one, it’s somewhat modular. You can unscrew the wood paneling on the front and replace it with attachments such as a small shelf for placing drinks or snacks.

The lid is fully detachable and reversible, so you can pop the whole thing off and get a full look at everything inside. Beyond this, dual-zone cooling is powerful. Each section can work as either a fridge or freezer.

And if you don’t need separate sections, the internal divider comes out, converting the entire interior to one large space at the same temperature. Travoca also sells internal baskets separately for easier organization.

Dometic is the best-known brand of portable refrigerators, with a reputation for turning out models that are durable and reliable With that comes the higher price tag, but overlanders and outdoor enthusiasts are still fans—I see this one touted most in forums as the main fridge people use while traveling on long remote treks.

It’s on the heavier side at 60 pounds when empty, but its compressor is more powerful than other models on this list—and it operates quietly.

The portable refrigerator has a sleek display and an intuitive app to set and keep tabs on the interior temperature, plus a USB port for charging for mobile devices.

With a wheeled base and telescopic handles, this portable fridge from BougeRV is a well-built mix between portability and size. The interior comes with two separate sections. You can tune each to different temperatures, allowing you to have both a functional fridge and freezer at the same time.

One of the more user-friendly features the CRD2 has is an opening for a standalone battery. While sold separately, the battery allows the cooler to operate without any large power source, like a wall outlet or car, nearby. With the attached battery, the portable fridge can run for up to 20 hours with no other power source, making it an ideal way to escape to the beach or sleep overnight in the woods away from your car and still wake up to fresh produce and unspoiled milk.

Portable refrigerators run on a compressor just like your kitchen fridge and freezer and keep food fresher a lot longer than a cooler and ice. Most reach an average minimum temperature of -4 to -7 degrees Fahrenheit to freeze and refrigerate food, though some are refrigerators only, reaching a minimum temperature of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

Although portable refrigerators don't rely solely on insulation for cooling power, they're still well insulated enough to take some of the load off the compressor when it comes to temperature regulation.

Don’t confuse portable refrigerators with electric coolers, as that’s another product category entirely. Electric coolers rely on thermoelectric cooling, which isn’t as efficient because it's impacted by ambient temperatures. As such, they can only cool to about 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Unlike portable refrigerators, electric coolers don’t have a compressor and don’t have the power to achieve freezing temperatures.

Portable refrigerators typically draw an average of about 45 watts of power, which is less than a standard mini fridge. This won’t blow out any car fuses or drain a car battery unless the unit is kept on for days without the car running. We chose portable refrigerators that have features like eco modes and automatic shutoff so there are precautions in place to prevent it from draining a car or portable battery.

While portable refrigerators offer more storage than coolers because they don’t need ice, their built-in compressor makes them relatively heavy at about 30 pounds or more. Still, some are more portable than others thanks to built-in handles and wheels. They don’t have shoulder straps and aren’t meant to be carried over a far distance. Also, most don't have drain plugs like standard coolers because condensation is minimal and can easily be wiped out with a small towel.

#6231. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.
