#6169. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6168. United Airlines Remembers Your Bad Flight And May Upgrade You Next Time

United Airlines appears to be quietly remembering when passengers suffer through a bad trip and then surprising some of them with a complimentary Economy Plus seat on a future flight. It costs United very little when the seat would otherwise remain empty, but it communicates something valuable to the passenger: we remember what happened to you.

A passenger recently shared an interesting message from United Airlines with aviation insider JonNYC.

The traveler had missed a connection about a month earlier and then received the following message before another United flight:

“We know your previous travel experience may have faced some challenges, and we want to make your journey more comfortable.”

United moved the passenger to Economy Plus, offering additional legroom at no charge.

United:personally, dunno if this is new/true/previously reported:

"think this could be of interest to you- UA IT has pulled some more dark magic, systems are starting to remember a bad IROP a pax went through (I misconnected a month ago). Received this before my flight… pic.twitter.com/isS2SvsQcj

What makes the gesture especially interesting is that the passenger had no MileagePlus elite status. The upcoming flight was lightly booked, which presumably made it easier for United to offer the seat without giving up revenue.

JonNYC described it as United’s technology performing more “dark magic,” and I think that is a fair description. The system appears to have connected an earlier operational disruption with a future reservation, then identified an inexpensive opportunity to improve the next journey.

Reports of similar gestures stretch back at least to 2025, so this does not appear to be entirely new. One United Silver member reported receiving an Economy Plus assignment after an eight-hour delay, even after United had already provided a $75 travel credit.

But United has not publicly announced this as a formal benefit, and we do not know precisely how passengers are selected (not that I would expect otherwise with such a “Surprise and Delight” program, lest it become an entitlement).

With advancing technology, airlines already know when they have inconvenienced you.

They know when your flight was delayed, when you missed a connection, and when you were rebooked. They also know whether you have another reservation and which seats remain available on that flight.

Yet customers are often forced to explain the entire situation again in a complaint, including information the airline already has in its own systems. That creates more work for the passenger after the airline has already disrupted the trip, though I’m sadly not expecting carriers to offer proactive compensation, even when delays are within its control.

United appears to be using its data more intelligently, like with its ConnectionSaver technology, that can help some passengers without inconveniencing others.

I have written before about United introducing technology that saves callers from repeating information when they are transferred from an automated system to a human agent. I also welcomed the addition of an app feature that watches earlier flights for disrupted passengers while preserving their confirmed reservations.

This Economy Plus gesture reflects a similar approach: use the information already available to reduce friction and improve the passenger experience.

An Economy Plus seat is not a first class upgrade. The passenger receives more legroom, but the onboard service remains the same as regular economy class.

Even so, it has value. United charges for these seats, sometimes quite a bit depending upon the route and seat location. Receiving one unexpectedly can make a future flight noticeably more comfortable.

The economics also make sense for United. If the flight is lightly booked and the Economy Plus seat would otherwise remain empty, the marginal cost of assigning it to an inconvenienced passenger is essentially zero.

The value to the passenger can be much greater than the cost to the airline.

I also appreciate that the message explicitly connects the better seat to the previous experience. A random seat reassignment might go unnoticed, while a clearly explained gesture tells the passenger that United remembers what happened and wants another chance to deliver a better trip.

That is smart service recovery…I wonder if the system is smart enough to do this when passengers have to be moved anyway due to weight and balance reasons? (why let a good opportunity go to waste?)

This is not a published benefit, and passengers should not expect a complimentary Economy Plus assignment every time something goes wrong. We do not know what level of disruption qualifies, how much empty space must be available, or whether United considers the passenger’s fare or travel history…and that’s the point, lest it become an expectation.

And of course United must be careful when selecting a seat to avoid a familiar complaint on Delta Air Lines. Moving someone from a regular economy aisle seat to an Economy Plus middle seat will not strike every passenger as an improvement. Ideally, the system should preserve the passenger’s aisle or window preference whenever possible or offer the upgrade rather than automatically moving the traveler.

Furthermore, if a MileagePlus Premier is expecting an entire row and suddenly has a seatmate, I can understand there will be annoyance (though that’s a sort of entitlement that is not helpful either)…in the past I’ve passed on upgrades to domestic first class in order to stretch across multiple seats in economy class.

Still, those limitations do not diminish the appeal of the idea. This is a discretionary gesture, not something passengers can demand, and that element of surprise is part of what makes it effective.

When airlines discuss service recovery, the conversation often centers on travel credits or miles. Those can be appropriate, particularly after a serious operational failure. But compensation need not be limited to those forms.

A better seat, lounge invitation, meal voucher, or another small benefit can communicate recognition when it is offered thoughtfully. The key is identifying something the passenger will appreciate that the airline can provide at a modest cost.

United has become particularly skilled at using technology to address operational problems. ConnectionSaver is the best example, intelligently holding certain flights when connecting passengers can reach the gate without causing a significant delay.

United appears to be quietly offering complimentary Economy Plus seats to some passengers whose previous trips went poorly, including travelers without elite status.

The gesture will not erase a missed connection or make every passenger forget a miserable journey. But it shows that United remembers the disruption and recognizes an opportunity to do something helpful. An empty Economy Plus seat costs United almost nothing. Used this way, it can generate far more goodwill than another automated apology email…it’s a positive step.

…and also why I avoid skiplagging on United! 😉

#6167. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6166. Ryanair Delays Free Seat Assignments, Says Passengers Who Don’t Pay “Clearly Don’t Mind Where They Sit”

Ryanair passengers who decline to pay for seat selection must now wait until only a few hours before departure to learn where they will sit. The airline says the change preserves more choice for customers willing to pay, which makes commercial sense. It also creates another incentive to purchase a seat simply to end the uncertainty.

Ryanair has changed when it assigns complimentary random seats to passengers who do not purchase one.

Previously, passengers generally received their seat assignment when checking in up to 24 hours before departure. Under the new approach, the seat may not appear on the digital boarding pass until approximately three to four hours before the flight.

The change was introduced with Ryanair’s winter schedule at the end of October.

Passengers can still check in beginning 72 hours before departure, but those who decline to pay for a seat may have to wait until the day of travel for the airline to update their boarding pass with an actual seat assignment.

Ryanair told RTE that it received complaints from passengers who wanted to purchase a particular seat on the day of departure, only to find that desirable seats had already been distributed through free random allocation.

Its explanation included a very Ryanair-like observation:

“Passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit.”

Therefore, Ryanair now keeps more seats available for purchase until closer to departure. Passengers who have selected random seating will have their digital boarding passes automatically updated once the airline assigns them a seat.

The logic is understandable: if someone is willing to pay for an aisle or window seat three hours before departure, Ryanair would rather sell it than discover it gave that seat away for free the previous evening. But let’s not pretend that preserving customer choice is the only objective here…those who are going to buy a seat usually do so in advance, so we are only talking about last-minute purchases.

I have no problem with Ryanair charging for advance seat assignments. That is the low-cost carrier “unbundled” model: advertise a very inexpensive base fare and allow passengers to decide which extras are worth purchasing.

I have flown Ryanair many times and approach it with those expectations. If I care where I sit, I pay. If I do not, I take whatever the airline gives me (of course hoping I end up with a window or aisle seat).

But the timing of this change creates pressure that did not exist before. A passenger can complete check-in yet remain uncertain about the seat assignment until shortly before leaving for the airport. Some will become impatient or anxious and pay simply to resolve it.

That is certainly good ancillary-revenue strategy. It is also another example of Ryanair understanding exactly how to monetize uncertainty. The airline knows that passengers become increasingly willing to spend as departure approaches. A middle seat may be tolerable when the trip is weeks away, but somehow looks much less appealing on the morning of the flight.

Ryanair’s family seating policy remains important here.

Under the airline’s published policy, children between two and 11 years old must be seated beside at least one accompanying adult. The adult is required to reserve a seat, while up to four children receive adjacent reserved seats without an additional seat-selection charge. Additional adults and passengers aged 12 or older who do not purchase seats may be assigned elsewhere.

Families should be aware that they are not guaranteed to be seated next to eachother (and it would not surprise me if the Ryanair algorithm specially avoids this in order to encourage famlies to pre-pay for seats on the next trip).

Ryanair now waits until approximately three to four hours before departure to assign complimentary random seats, allowing it to preserve more desirable inventory for passengers willing to pay.

The commercial reasoning is clear, and I do not fault Ryanair for selling seat assignments. But delaying the free assignment also creates anxiety that will persuade some passengers to purchase a seat they otherwise would not have bought. It is clever revenue management, but hardly an improvement for passengers.

And while we are on the topic of Ryanair, can I just say how much I loved this tweet:

they fired the CEO with the same confidence you say "never flying Ryanair again" https://t.co/s63NRElFlI

#6165. Delta Outage Delays Hundreds of Flights

A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

Delta said in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

The FAA said on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg

The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

While resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

#6163. Lufthansa Turns Airplane Etiquette Into Clothing

Lufthansa is turning airplane etiquette into a clothing collection, including a new shirt reminding passengers that there is no need to stand up immediately after landing. I like the idea and agree with much of the advice, though standing up is not necessarily the problem…pushing past everyone else is.

Lufthansa has announced that four items from its Travel Etiquette Collection will go on sale through the WorldShop beginning November 27, 2026.

The collection debuted in August and was not originally intended for sale. Lufthansa says the response prompted a retail edition, including a new shirt based on the most popular suggestion from its social media community.

Each design is limited to 250 individually numbered pieces. Lufthansa will donate its licensing proceeds to help alliance, the Lufthansa Group’s aid organization (that is the licensing revenue, rather than necessarily the entire purchase price).

Prices were not included in the announcement.

First off, I love these…simple yet stylish.

As to the messaging itself, I understand why the shirt appeals to people. We have all watched passengers spring up as though standing in the aisle will somehow make the jet bridge attach faster.

And if the aircraft is still moving or the seatbelt sign remains illuminated, it should go without saying that you stay seated.

But once the aircraft is parked and passengers are permitted to get up, I have no objection to someone standing. After several hours in an economy class seat, stretching your legs is perfectly understandable. An aisle passenger can also retrieve a bag and be ready to leave when the rows ahead have cleared.

The problem is the person who charges forward from row 28 and wedges himself beside row 19, apparently convinced that everyone else is sitting there for his convenience.

Stand if you want. Just wait your turn to leave.

(The only exception I would make are the circumstances in which the crew asks passengers to remain seated so travelers with tight connections can get off first. That requires everyone to cooperate, including those of us who might otherwise prefer to stand…but I also have a problem with the “free riders” in those situations…another issue for another day.)

My favorite in this collection is the “Recline Responsibly” message, which strikes me as common sense, but something so many passengers are so rude about.

If an airline installs a reclining seat, passengers should generally be able to use that feature. But look behind you first and recline slowly. Giving the person behind you a moment to adjust a laptop or move a drink costs you very little.

During meal service, the seat should be upright, but other than that, recline away…just gently.

We spend so much time arguing about whether reclining is acceptable that we sometimes overlook how much the manner of doing it matters. A slow adjustment is very different from throwing your seat back without warning.

Lufthansa will begin selling four limited-edition etiquette items on November 27. I like the collection, particularly the reminder to recline responsibly. But I can’t say I’ll be up late waiting to buy it…how about you?

#6162. No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, New Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

#6161. “We Have Had Alien Sightings Out There” ATC Tells American Eagle Pilot After Unexplained Traffic Alert

An American Eagle pilot asked air traffic control about an unexplained traffic advisory near Baltimore and received an answer that probably was not what he was expecting: there had been “alien sightings” in the area. The exchange makes for entertaining listening, though the actual report is considerably less dramatic.

A recording circulating online captures an unusual conversation reportedly involving American Eagle flight 5432 from Washington National (DCA) to Philadelphia (PHL) on November 21, 2026.

According to International Business Times, PSA Airlines operated the flight with a Bombardier CRJ-900, using the callsign Blue Streak 5432. Near Baltimore, the pilot asked about a traffic advisory without an identification tag. The controller explained that the flight had already passed the only other known traffic nearby.

“I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…”

The controller went on to describe an earlier report from another pilot about something zigzagging ahead of an aircraft near Martin State Airport, without a corresponding radar target.

The American Eagle pilot took the comment in good humor, suggesting it would make an interesting story to tell his family.

A pilot reporting strange lights near Baltimore got an unexpected response from ATC, who casually mentioned there had been alien sightings in the area. The pilot joked that he’d have quite the story to tell his family. 👽✈️#ATC #Aviation #Aliens pic.twitter.com/rtalRieUwH

— Flightdrama (@flightdrama) November 21, 2026

Before you start booking a window seat from BWI specifically to look for visitors from another planet, the American Eagle crew was asking about a traffic advisory… these pilots did not actually see an unidentified object outside their aircraft.

The zigzagging object was part of the controller’s recollection of a different pilot’s report: there’s quite a leap from an unexplained alert and a controller’s remark to an extraterrestrial encounter.

Yet after so much grim aviation news lately, I enjoyed this one.

Pilots and controllers have serious responsibilities, but there is room for a little personality on the frequency when circumstances permit. It is often the testy verbal exchanges between pilots and air traffic controllers that make headlines, but a passing remark like this also gives us a glimpse of the human beings doing the work.

An American Eagle pilot’s question about a traffic advisory prompted an unexpected reference to earlier alien sightings near Baltimore. While there was no alien spacecraft sighting, it is an entertaining radio exchange and a rather good story.

#6159. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6158. Review: Air France A350-900 Business Class Paris To New York

Air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to New York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

This was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

My journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

Far more important the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

There are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

This is one of my favorite business class seats.

Air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:

The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):

Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

Admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

It was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

The entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV shows, games, and music.

Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

Fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

Service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

The new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

We landed on time at JFK, and I quickly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in New York.

Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh…

This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

Air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

#6157. Deranged American Airlines Passenger Screams “I Want To See Jesus” And Tries To Rip Open Emergency Exit Door Before Fellow Travelers Restrain Him With Zip Ties And Duct Tape

Passengers and flight attendants worked together to restrain a man with zip ties and duct tape after he allegedly tried to open an exit door on an American Airlines flight to Chicago. The aircraft diverted to Phoenix, and the FBI says the man is now in custody. A frightening start to Thanksgiving travel, but also a reminder of how quickly strangers can come together when help is needed.

American Airlines flight 1494 was traveling from San Diego (SAN) to Chicago O’Hare (ORD) when a passenger disturbance forced a diversion to Phoenix (PHX) early on November 25, 2026.

According to Phoenix police, the man left his seat, moved toward the front of the aircraft, refused instructions to sit down, and attempted to tamper with an exit door.

Flight attendants and passengers restrained him until the aircraft landed safely in Phoenix around 1:00 am. The man sustained a minor injury and was taken to a hospital for evaluation. No injuries were reported among the other passengers or crew. Take a look at these videos:

Passenger Sean Bennett, who posted the videos above, said that he had been sleeping when a flight attendant’s shouting woke him. Another passenger, Hunter Glegory, recalled the man saying:

“I want to see Jesus, get me off this plane.”

.Passenger video captured the struggle and the use of zip ties and duct tape. One witness also described a flight attendant using a beverage cart to keep the confrontation from moving farther down the aisle. The FBI subsequently confirmed that the man had been taken into custody. It is interviewing witnesses and consulting federal prosecutors about possible charges.

Passengers eventually continued to Chicago later Wednesday.

Imagine waking up on a redeye to a flight attendant shouting at someone to get away from a door (I had one such experience many years ago…).

You are tired, perhaps disoriented, and suddenly trying to understand whether the commotion ahead is something that threatens you or your family. I would find that deeply unsettling and am thankful passengers were willing to help the crew.

Flight attendants are trained to respond to disturbances, but physically restraining someone who continues to resist can require assistance. People who had boarded simply planning on waking up in Chicago found themselves helping contain a dangerous situation instead.

We often focus on the selfish behavior we encounter onboard, and there is certainly no shortage of material. But here we saw passengers stepping forward to help people they did not know. Others described a remarkably calm response around them.

As we celebrate Thanksgiving in the USA, that is something to appreciate.

The reported remark about wanting to see Jesus is disturbing in this context, but it is not clear whether the man was experiencing a medical crisis, was under the influence of something, or acted for another reason. Whatever the explanation, the crew had to address his conduct immediately. Compassion for someone who may be in distress and firm action to protect everyone onboard are entirely compatible.

I hope the investigation establishes what happened and that the man receives appropriate care if he needs it and faces justice if this was due to a controllable choice like drugs or alcohol. I also hope the passengers and crew who intervened are doing well. AA should also send this guy the bill for the extra fuel, crew time, and anything other related expenses.

An American Airlines redeye to Chicago diverted to Phoenix after a passenger allegedly tampered with an exit door and refused crew instructions. Passengers helped flight attendants restrain him, and the FBI is now investigating.

A lot of people had their holiday journey disrupted, but the aircraft landed safely and no other passengers or crew were reported injured. Credit to the crew and those who helped them. None of those passengers signed up to spend the night restraining a stranger, but when assistance was needed, they stepped forward.

#6156. Storms on Both Coasts Threaten Thanksgiving Travel

Powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

In the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG

Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency said.

NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

For New York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

In California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A new system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

The impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor said residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists said.

Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

#6155. Giving Thanks When America Feels Like The Last Days Of Narnia

This Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia. Not because I believe the world is ending, but because C.S. Lewis understood how easily faith can be exploited by those seeking power…and how difficult it becomes to see clearly when we are frightened or angry.

In The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned. Shift then speaks for him, demanding obedience and using their love for Aslan to advance his own interests.

The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful. They have difficulty believing that someone invoking Aslan could be asking them to betray everything Aslan represents.

I find that painfully familiar when I watch Christians excuse conduct in Donald Trump that they would rightly condemn in almost anyone else. Once defending a leader becomes a religious obligation, we have given him something that never belonged to him.

The lion’s skin does not make the donkey Aslan. Invoking Christianity does not make a political demand Christian.

That warning applies to me too. Seeing another person’s hypocrisy does not excuse my own contempt. Being right about a political failure does not make every word I write about it righteous.

I can become so occupied with what is wrong that I stop noticing what God has given me. I can begin to enjoy indignation. That is a dangerous habit for anyone, particularly someone who writes for a living.

Scripture takes ingratitude seriously. In Romans 1:21, Paul describes people who knew God but neither honored Him as God nor gave thanks. Ingratitude accompanies their descent into darkened thinking and idolatry. And in Ephesians 5:3–4, Paul places thanksgiving where corrupt speech ought to be displaced. Gratitude is part of how we resist sin.

Giving thanks reminds me that I am a recipient of mercy. I have no grounds to treat another person as beyond its reach.

I remain grateful to be an American. I will continue to criticize our government when I believe it deserves criticism, and I will continue to pray for those who govern us, including President Trump.

But my allegiance belongs to the Kingdom of Heaven and to Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. No party gets to borrow that allegiance. No president gets to claim it.

That gives me freedom to acknowledge something good done by someone I oppose and something wrong done by someone I supported. It also means an election cannot deliver everything I hope for or take away everything that matters.

Paul tells Christians to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). I understand that to include circumstances I want to change. Gratitude does not require pretending that injustice is good or that incompetence is harmless.

Today, I am thankful for my wife and children, for the church that has sustained me, my loving and supportive family and friends, and for the extraordinary privilege of traveling through this world and sharing it with you. Most of all, I am thankful that my hope rests with a King whose character does not require excuses.

Lewis understood that Shift did not have the last word. I need to remember that too.

#6154. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6152. United Airlines CEO Says “The Lead That We Have Is Going To Grow” In Thanksgiving Message To Employees

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world. But his most revealing comment concerned what comes next: he expects United to widen its lead over every other airline.

In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.

He also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them. That was the most predictable and customary part of a Thanksgiving message, though Kirby could not resist adding a competitive prediction.

Kirby again called United the best airline in the world, then told employees:

“I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines.”

That is quite a statement, particularly the reference to all other airlines rather than just American or Delta.

I increasingly enjoy flying United. I recently wrote about how Starlink influences which flights I book, and my experiences with the crews and operation have generally been very positive too. Even as a free agent, I find myself drawn back to United. That is a good position for an airline to be in: winning my business because I like the flight it offers rather than because I need another qualifying dollar toward elite status.

But calling United the best airline in the world remains a much broader claim than I would make. My recent Air France A350 business class flight, for example, offered a level of comfort and dining that United would struggle to match consistently.

United also still has a wide variation in its onboard product. An A321neo with Starlink and a comfortable cabin presents a very different experience from an older aircraft with unreliable internet.

We can all understand why Kirby speaks this way to employees. He wants them to take pride in the airline and believe that their work is building something better. But the claim becomes more persuasive when passengers can board any aircraft in the fleet and reasonably expect a similarly good experience. That may be coming, but United is still quite a ways off.

What I appreciated most was Kirby’s emphasis on the individual employees who make travel easier.

A new cabin or faster internet can influence which flight I book. The way an employee treats me often determines how I feel about that flight afterward and critically to airlines, whether I would recommend it to others (part of the NPS score)

That becomes especially apparent when something goes wrong. A delay is frustrating, but an empathetic employee can preserve a lot of goodwill. Being ignored or brushed aside can turn an ordinary disruption into a reason to book another airline next time, which is a frequent issue for me on American Airlines.

Kirby says customers tell him about those positive encounters, including on the flight he took that day. It also connects with his recent message after the FAA ground stop, when he highlighted a crew helping a mother traveling with three young children. These are the experiences passengers remember, sometimes long after they have forgotten what they ate or which aircraft operated the flight.

Happy Thanksgiving everyone! At United, we’re about connecting people and uniting the world and that’s never more true than over the Thanksgiving holiday when we’re about to have our two busiest days of the travel period. I know many of you are going be working hard at the holidays and missing time with your friends and family so I want to say thank you for doing that and really taking care of our customer during this important time.

As we enter the Thanksgiving holiday, I’m thankful for an awful lot of things in my personal life but in my professional life, I’m thankful for all that you have done in the last several years to make United Airlines the best airline in the world. I fly a lot, including on my flight today, customers constantly are telling me stories about what a flight attendant or a pilot or a gate agent has done to ease their travel to do something special for them that makes a memory for them. So thank you for all you’ve done in the past several years to vault us to a leadership position.

Thank you for everything you’re doing right now during the holidays to take care of customers and I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines. Thank you for really doing things to not just make United Airlines the best in the world but to set a new standard for what it means to be a great airline in global aviation. Happy Thanksgiving and thank you.

Kirby is thankful for the employees who he believes have made United the best airline in the world, and he expects its lead over competitors to grow.

I share his enthusiasm for much of what United is doing, though I am not ready to award it that title. The more compelling part of his message was the recognition that employees earn customer loyalty through the way they treat people.

United has given me plenty of reasons to return lately. Continuing to deliver those good experiences will do far more to persuade me than any declaration that it is already the best. To everyone working at the airport or onboard today, thank you. I hope passengers remember that the person helping them get home may be spending the holiday away from their own family.

#6151. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6150. A Thanksgiving Resolution

The boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race. But he noticed something else, something troubling.

Humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself. Not just wars of weaponry and nation states, but deeper wars of ideas and values. Like a cancer imperfectly treated, the pestilence of irreconcilable division ebbed and flowed…but perpetually manifested itself in fierce battles and spilled blood.

The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was. A humanitarian? A missionary? A soldier? A politician? A writer? A peacemaker? Perhaps a little of each. Perhaps none of the above. He married a woman from a different culture and with a different worldview. The challenge of marriage personified the challenge of the surrounding world — putting differences asides to build trust, loyalty, and respect while growing in love and patience. Was this even possible absent divine intervention?

Then one Thanksgiving Day it hit him. He could not change the world. Not alone anyway. But there was one one thing he could do, something so trite on the one hand but absolutely revolutionary on the other: he could love his neighbor as he loved himself.

Just how would that look? Being honest, generous, forgiving, joyful, peaceful, patient, kind, and faithful to everyone he encountered. He would often fail, but it became a primary goal in life.

The man still ponders his place in this world, but there is one thing he knows — there may be many things he is not, but he is a traveler and that gives him a unique opportunity to put his maxim to practice in venues far beyond the friendly confines of home. Blessed with so much through circumstance of birth, he pauses to reflect upon the blessings he has been the recipient of, many from those who follow a similar maxim.

Perhaps one day you will meet him and he can encourage you or share in your struggles. His goal is to leave every person he crosses paths with knowing that they are loved and respected. Life is often unkind and this goal is insurmountable in all places and at all times, but it is worth pursuing.

Now, he invites you to join him in his journey to put others before himself. One day and one person at a time, humanity can tame the inhumane world it finds itself in.

This post has appeared annually on Thanksgiving Day since 2015.

#6147. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.
