#6126. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

There's no doubt about it: The airport lounge wars are heating up with credit card issuers like American Express, Capital One and Chase launching new outposts at a blistering pace.

American Express maintains the largest footprint with its Global Lounge Collection, while Capital One has been expanding its map of Capital One airport lounges.

However, it's Chase in particular that has turned up the heat, expanding its U.S. lounge collection since 2023, with more on the way, including a location at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Here’s everything you need to know about the family of Chase Sapphire Lounges by The Club, their amenities and how to access them.

Apply for the : Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (see ).

Chase’s lounge collection includes nine Sapphire Lounge locations. The JFK location is temporarily closed.

Additional lounges are planned at the following airports:

Chase has partnered with Airport Dimensions to build out its lounges. Airport Dimensions currently operates dozens of lounges worldwide, most of which are branded as “The Club” or “Club Aspire” and are largely accessible via Priority Pass membership.

Related: Is a Priority Pass lounge membership actually worth it?

This location was the first branded Chase lounge to open in the U.S.

It's located in the Terminal B-to-C connector near gates B39 and B40 and is accessible post-security from Terminals B, C and E. Passengers departing from Terminal A will need to clear security again when returning to their departure terminal.

The lounge has an expansive footprint, at over 11,000 square feet with seating for over 200 guests, though lines to get in can certainly form at busy times, with waits topping an hour. It is open from 5 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

In addition to a variety of restaurant- and living room-style seating areas, there is a self-serve buffet at one end. Guests can also order a la carte dishes created by Boston-area chef Douglass Williams as well as specialty cocktails and Massachusetts-brewed beers from table-mounted QR codes.

The lounge also has wellness rooms with massage chairs and comfortable loungers for relaxation and products from Brooklyn-based fragrance brand Apotheke.

The newest Chase Sapphire Lounge opened at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in July 2026. Located post-security near gate D25 in Terminal D, the 18,000-square-foot lounge is one of the largest in the Sapphire network. It is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

In addition to Chase's signature made-to-order dining (with dishes like blue corn butterscotch pancakes from favorite local restaurant Encina), an all-day buffet and full-service bar, the DFW location introduces several features unique to the network. Travelers can visit the first dedicated Sapphire whiskey lounge featuring guided tastings of Texas whiskeys (and a specialty honey pecan Old Fashioned cocktail), book a complimentary 30-minute Face Haus treatment, freshen up in a shower suite or relax in dedicated rest areas.

Families will also appreciate the children's play area and private nursing room, while travelers in a hurry can take advantage of a grab-and-go food station — a feature Chase is currently testing at this location.

Chase and Airport Dimensions revamped The Etihad Lounge at Dulles, located in Concourse A near gate A14.

The space is small, at just over 5,000 square feet, but features two levels with various seating areas, including a library-themed space, gender-neutral restrooms, shower suites, a reflection room for quiet meditation and a family room.

As with the other lounge locations, this one features locally-inspired food and cocktails plus locally-brewed java from Commonwealth Joe Coffee Roasters.

The lounge is currently open from 6 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

Chase's lounge at LAS is located past security in Terminal 1, Concourse C, between gates 23 and 24. It opened in December 2025, spans two stories, covers 4,590 square feet and has seating for up to 87 people. It is open from 4:30 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

Though compact compared to the other Chase Sapphire lounges, this one packs a punch in terms of ambience. The space features colorful artwork and a lively atmosphere, not to mention a rather glamorous "Champagne parlor" plus a menu of cocktails inspired by Sin City and a wine list curated by New York retailer Parcelle.

Food options include bites like pork buns and a spicy cucumber salad from Momofuku.

There are no showers, spa services or meditation rooms here, though.

The issuer is bringing a lounge to LAX on an unconfirmed date. It will be adjacent to gate 148 near the connector to the west gates at Tom Bradley International Terminal.

Now that all terminals at LAX are connected airside (post-security), any traveler with access could theoretically visit this lounge, although it is a bit of a hike from other terminals.

The new lounge will measure around 9,000 square feet, which is on the smaller side — especially for an airport the size of LAX — so expect some long wait times once it opens, much as you'll find at the nearby Centurion Lounge.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge by The Club at JFK is located in Terminal 4 near gate A2, not far from the security checkpoint and up one level.

Like the location at IAD, this space is a redesigned Etihad Lounge rather than one Chase created from scratch, and it's rather limited in size at just 7,600 square feet.

It is usually open from 4:30 a.m. until 9 p.m. daily, but at the time of publication, it is temporarily closed due to plumbing issues. There are grab-and-go food options, though.

Typically, you can find a buffet of small plates, plus seasonal items (but always the famous burger) available for order via QR code. This lounge also has three shower suites.

The LaGuardia Sapphire Lounge is the largest of the collection, at 21,000 square feet spanning two floors. It is located in Terminal B and is open from 4:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. daily.

The lounge houses plenty of spacious seating areas, including a restaurant-style section and more casual vignettes. There are also family-oriented areas, including a children's playroom and arcade.

The lounge offers a buffet and a seasonal menu featuring select dishes from Sailor, a restaurant in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, plus locally inspired cocktails by Apotheke and wines chosen by Parcelle.

There's also a wellness area where guests can enjoy Face Haus facial treatments, guided meditations from podcaster Devi Brown and private rest pods.

Uniquely, the lounge features Reserve Suites, Chase’s lounge-within-a-lounge concept, which you can reserve for $2,200-$3,000 for a three-hour private retreat.

This 20,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in February 2025 in the connector between Terminal D (home of Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Spirit Airlines, Alaska Airlines and United Airlines) and Terminal E (where gates for Frontier Airlines, JetBlue, Alaska Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Spirit Airlines can be found).

If you go through the Terminal D Transportation Security Administration checkpoint, it is upstairs and is open from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily.

It offers a similar layout to other Chase lounges, but with some unique features including a wellness center with two treatment rooms for facials, two shower suites, a game room, Elixr Coffee drinks and a bar with Philadelphia Eagles-themed cocktails, plus a beer garden and local dishes courtesy of Fishtown eatery Middle Child Clubhouse.

The Sapphire Lounge at PHX opened in November 2024 and is located at the new eight-gate facility in Terminal 4 near gate D11.

This lounge began accepting reservations in June 2025. Sapphire Reserve cardmembers departing from Phoenix can reserve their visit from 14 days up to 24 hours before arriving at the lounge, so you don't have to be physically present to make your reservation. That's because this is the smallest lounge, at just 3,500 square feet.

The lounge is open from 4:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. daily, though its site notes that hours may vary.

There are a few different seating areas, with the tables around the central cocktail bar being in high demand. There's also an indoor terrace separated from the terminal, where a retrofitted Airstream food truck serves specialties from Gallo Blanco. Guests will also find Arizona-based Press Coffee drinks on hand, craft cocktails and a Parcelle-selected list of wines.

Located in San Diego's Terminal 2, this 11,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in December 2024 with plenty of surfer-themed art and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the tarmac.

The lounge is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily and has a swanky wraparound cocktail bar, a small buffet area (plus à la carte dishes by Oscars Mexican Seafood on offer via QR code) and plenty of distinct seating areas.

There's also a wellness area with four relaxation pods and Face Haus treatments, a family room, showers and a nursing room.

Chase is planning a new 16,000-square-foot Sapphire Lounge in Concourse A at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The Port of Seattle approved the project in October 2026, with a planned $70 million investment covering the initial build-out and a future refurbishment. An opening date has not yet been announced.

Related: 5 ways to ensure you have lounge access before your next flight

Those with the (see rates and fees), (see rates and fees), J.P. Morgan Reserve or Ritz-Carlton™ Credit Card can access these lounges.

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card and the Ritz-Carlton Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Cardholders can access the lounges up to three hours before departure (or up to five hours before a connecting flight) and can also bring up to two guests per visit for free. If you're a cardholder and wish to bring more than two guests, you'll be charged a fee. Children under 2 can enter for free.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve review: A premium card for power travelers

While Priority Pass members previously got to access a Chase Lounge once per calendar year, this benefit has been discontinued.

Select Etihad travelers (the airline’s Gold and Platinum elite members and those flying in business or first class on Etihad-operated flights) can visit the IAD and JFK locations before their flights.

Related: A guide to guest policies for airport lounges

For years, Amex's network of Centurion Lounges was the major player in the card-run lounge space, but in recent years, Chase has quickly caught up, opening a series of lounges around the country in record time, with more on the way. With the airport lounge competition intensifying among major credit card issuers, the real winners are cardholders, though.

That said, these lounges feel like they're getting more crowded by the day, so when you get to an airport with one, make a beeline to the entrance and put your name on the list for access just in case there's a wait. After all, you wouldn't want to miss out on their many amenities.

#6124. 40% Off Away Promo Code | November 2026

It’s no secret that Away is one of our team's favorite luggage brands. With its thoughtfully designed suitcases and sleek essentials, the brand has become synonymous with effortless movement, whether you’re heading out on a quick city escape or a long-haul adventure.

If you’ve been waiting to invest in your next travel companion, know that verified Away promo codes and Black Friday sales can help you save on signature styles—from up to $100 off select luggage bundles to 25% off sitewide and an extra 10% off purchases over $750. Whether you’re planning a cross-country road trip or a flight abroad, these savings make it easier to pack stylishly and travel smarter.

Black Friday is almost here, and Away's biggest sale of the year is live. Shoppers can take 25% off sitewide (the one major exclusion: the Series 3 collection), which nets out to as much as $186 per item. This sale runs through 11:59 PM PST on December 1, or the date on which supplies run out, so you've got a little time to decide. You can also shop in stores if you prefer and score the same discount. Not sure what to get? If I were in the market for a new carry-on, I'd go with the Bigger Carry-On—in fact, I recently took it with me on a five-day trip. During the sale, it's $221 instead of $295.

Buying luggage for the whole family? If you spend $750 or more, you'll get 10% off the entire order. If you are shopping for multiple pieces, know that you can save even more by bundling items. There are a whole bunch of options that can help cut down on any holiday decision fatigue—the best-selling Jetsetter bundle saves you $255, with sets like the Work From Anywhere bundle or the Best Selling bundle saving you $124. There's also a build your own bundle option for those looking with specific items in mind.

Whichever route you go, you can rest easy knowing each piece is crafted for travelers who value both form and function: hard-shell suitcases that glide seamlessly through terminals, compact carry-ons with convenient compartments, and travel bags that make packing feel like an art.

For even steeper Black Friday discounts, head to Away's Last Chance sale page. As the name suggests, these items aren't coming back, so if there's something you like, don't dillydally (but also keep in mind that you won't be able to return it). There are a ton of fun pieces for kids in there, including a few items from the Toy Story collaboration. The Featherlight Weekender is marked down 30%, bringing its price tag down to $103, as is the ultra-chic Pet Carrier ($159, down from $228). The Softside Compact Carry-On is another great find, especially for business travelers or anyone looking to shift their personal item from a tote or backpack to a roller ($123, down from $205). One more item to call out, especially for those with football games or stadium concerts on their calendar—the clear Stadium Bag, which is 30% off in cherry red or island pink trim ($52, down from $75).

New customers, listen up: Away often offers a 10% off coupon on first orders when you sign up for emails and texts. This coupon code is not currently being offered, but keep your eyes peeled for its return. Once signed up, you'll stay in the loop on the latest launches and collabs, special events, and more. To snag the deal, head to Away's homepage and keep an out for a pop-up, then enter your information to sign up.

Away is making travel more accessible for those who give back to their communities with a 10% discount for veterans, active military members, medical personnel, teachers, and students. Whether you're a student preparing for a semester abroad or a teacher gearing up for a well-deserved getaway, this offer makes premium luggage more affordable. Simply verify your status through ID.me, and you’re all set to enjoy stylish, durable travel essentials at a discounted price. For more details, visit Away’s Hero Discounts.

Sharing your love of travel has its perks with Away’s $40 off referral offer. When you introduce a friend to the brand, they’ll receive $40 off their first purchase of $125 or more—and once their order is complete, you’ll get $40 off your next one, too. The best part? You can earn up to $200 in rewards by referring as many as five friends. To claim the offer, your friend simply uses your referral link to visit Away’s Get Rewarded page, where a unique code appears to apply at checkout. The discount is valid on suitcases and bags only, making it an ideal way to refresh your own travel setup while helping someone else discover the quality and design that make Away a go-to for savvy travelers.

Away proves that great design and thoughtful functionality don’t have to come at a steep price. #6123. The 40 Best Resorts in the Caribbean: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View this gallery as a list of the top resorts in the Caribbean with scores here.

The namesake hillside resort set above Toiny Bay gives “wild” an unexpected new meaning when it comes to sceney St. Barts. On the shrubby southeastern point of the island, this unfussy haven is where an in-the-know social set head to find serenity. The star amenity here is the private beach, accessible via a three-minute Defender ride down switchbacking roads. Le Toiny’s stretch of soft sand is considered the sole private hotel beach on all of St. Barts. Plus, some of the oldest traditional English-style cottages on the island, dating back to the 1700s, can be found beside the beach club (one is currently used as treatment areas for the spa). The suites and villas were redesigned in 2024 to create airy living spaces that draw your eye outward to the leafy open-air surroundings and azure water views just beyond your private pool deck.

Grand Cayman may be famous for its SCUBA diving and offshore banking, but with several daily non-stops from New York and Boston, it’s increasingly drawing families to its powdery, placid western Caribbean beaches. On the island’s Seven Mile Beach—one of the loveliest stretches of sand in the world—you'll find the 266-room Kimpton Seafire Resort & Spa, with a boutique atmosphere that manages to be both child-friendly (two pools, a kids club) and hip (colorful, contemporary design, and a lobby scene replete with pool table, library, and daily happy hour). The food is also strong: Hit beachside Coccoloba for fish tacos and ceviches; Ave, the resort's primary restaurant, for epic breakfast buffets (including house-made cronuts); and the sceney Avecita for progressive Spanish fare like white anchovy toast and prawn tartare, served up alongside craft cocktails at the chef’s counter. You can always snorkel and parasail right off the hotel’s beach, but you’re also just a short ride from Stingray City (where you can stand on a sandbar and touch giant rays as they swim by), world-class gardens (look for the endangered blue iguana), golf, and roadside jerk chicken. Hit Rum Point to toast the sunset—or maybe you'll prefer doing that from your own private balcony.

This romantic all-suite beachfront retreat north of the sprawling all-inclusives of Punta Cana is a diamond literally in the rough—the last two miles of the approach road are so bone rattling that it may be worth ponying up more than $250 for the ten-minute helicopter transfer from the airport in Punta Cana. But behind the resort’s unmarked security gate, Zoëtry is breathtaking. The open-air lobby has a soaring peaked thatch roof, and the 51rooms, divided between two-story thatched buildings and freestanding villas, are arranged around two snaking pools and are no more than a one-minute walk from the beach. With classic clean lines, they are dramatic by virtue of their size (the smallest is 775 square feet) and simple comforts—wicker ceilings, dark hardwood floors and furniture, white-on-white beds, immense bathrooms with black slate showers and deep soaking tubs. The resort’s restaurants draw culinary inspiration from traditional Dominican fare and international flavors, with an emphasis on using locally grown and organic ingredients.

For toes-in-the-sand luxury with impeccable service, foodie-approved eateries, Caribbean-cool rooms, and views that will have all your friends and family seeing green, La Samanna can’t be beat. Set along the white sands of Baie Longue, known for being one of the most beautiful beaches in all of St. Martin, guests are never far from the startlingly turquoise waters, and La Samanna offers plenty of ways to get out on the water, including complimentary kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and more. With three main restaurants—one of which changes in concept between lunch and dinner—plus a fabulous daily breakfast and top-notch room service, there’s really no reason to leave for meals. The star of the show is L’Oursin, the upscale French restaurant just off the lobby, where each table comes with a view of the sailboat-spotted sea. If you can, splurge on one of the property's eight independent villas—the double-level mansions have everything a group could need to vacation more than comfortably.

The "secret" part of Secret Bay's name is no accident—the resort's 10 gorgeous villas give new meaning to the word hideaway. Touches vary from villa to villa, but all have interiors and floors made of Guyanese Greenheart, bedroom furniture made of Dominican red cedar, open decks, private pools, and 180-degree views over the mountain peaks of Dominica and the Caribbean Sea. Though we doubt you'll get tired of living your own castaway fantasies (albeit with much nicer accommodations), Secret Bay's concierge is available to help craft personalized itineraries: think rainforest hikes with a famed naturalist, or a sunset sail along the island's western coast.

Anguilla is a small-but-mighty island packed with a handful of luxury properties, dining options, and a whole bunch of outstanding beaches. Barnes Bay and Meads Bay surround the property on both sides, with waters that are occasionally rough but known to be swimmable at other times of the year. Regardless of the conditions, white beach chairs line the sand in pristine formation each morning, and three large pool areas—two kid-friendly, and one adults-only—provide plenty of swimming options when the ocean is unavailable. The property stretches across the shore, which means each room provides a unique view of some combination of the wide property’s beachfront, ocean, palm trees, or garden areas. In the ocean-view one-bedroom suite, we overlooked the modernist pool deck as well as the distant ocean, with a plunge pool on the balcony and ample outdoor space for afternoon lounging. The bathroom was equipped with two sinks, a large tub, and a marble walk-in shower.

All rooms at this Sandals Resort are in stone buildings on a two-mile-long beach in a 500-acre wilderness preserve on the island's south coast. The resort is arranged as three European villages—Dutch, French, and Italian (including a Venetian piazza)—and the architecture includes lots of marble columns and vaulted ceilings. "Buildings are spread out, but it still feels like an intimate retreat." Rooms differ according to village: French rooms have mahogany four-poster beds and Caribbean decor, while Italian rooms are heavy on marble. The plantation-style Eleanor's, complete with a waterwheel and a stone fireplace, serves contemporary Caribbean cuisine.

Though the Buccaneer, on the U.S. Virgin Island of St. Croix, has been proudly run by the Armstrong family for over 70 years—it's the longest-running resort in the Caribbean—its history dates even further back to the property's earliest construction by a Knight of Malta in 1653. Since then, it's been a private home; a sugar mill; a cotton estate, then a cattle estate; and now, an incredibly warm, family-friendly resort that's more like a country club. You have access to an 18-hole golf course, eight tennis courts, three beaches (whether you prefer kayaking and snorkeling or lounging in peace and quiet), a full water sports center, and none of the pretense. Arrive for lunch at the Grotto in your bathing suit, and please don't sleep through the terrific breakfast buffet. The Buccanneer knows how to put out a spread. Once you're done moving about for the day, settle into the deluxe oceanfront room—the resort's most popular—and lie on your bed beneath the 16-foot-high wood ceilings, watching the waves lap the beach out your picture window.

The tiny volcanic island of Grenada is both an unexpected and obvious choice for Six Senses’ foray into the Caribbean. Compared to big-hitting neighbors like St. Lucia and Antigua, it has been overlooked by travelers to the region. But this means that it remains largely uncrowded and retains a more rustic version of tourism. Six Senses has done well to anchor itself to that. Here, your welcome ritual begins with a sensory spice “tour;” its 56 suites and 15 villas are stylish but designed to sit unobtrusively on the landscape; and its curated excursions—from rainforest hikes to Rastafarian farm visits—spotlight the best of Grenada’s natural bounty. In classic Six Senses style, wellness is a key protagonist, and you can seek out everything from aerial yoga to sleep therapy, as well as treatments like the Caribbean Cleansing Ritual that nod to the surroundings. It’s very tempting to stay put, heading to the spa or sipping rum cocktails poolside, but you’d do well to pair off with one of the property’s community hosts and head out: to spice-laden markets in its photogenic capital or for a bit of beachside limin’ (defined locally as “kicking with friends”), a beloved national pastime.

The old adage of getting what you pay for rings true here, and while it may be a splurge, it will be an unforgettable stay. The rooms are quiet, the beds are comfortable, and in my opinion, this is the best stretch of beach on the island. If you’re looking for luxury—and budget isn’t an issue—the Ritz is the top of the line. Guests who stay in the 320 spacious and chic rooms can expect to be spoiled. Servers cruise around the shore on Segway scooters, effortlessly balancing trays of tropical cocktails. The concierge can secure reservations for you at sold-out restaurants, set up offsite tours, and suggest itineraries for any kind of traveler. The 15,000-square-foot spa at the Ritz is one of the largest and best on the island, and the property's on-site restaurants are simply divine. The vibe is upscale without being stuffy, with guests in the elevators side by side wearing pool towels and Prada.

A relatively new addition to St. Barts' luxury hotel scene, Le Barthélemy is a sophisticated winner that keeps with the island's low-rise sensibility. Set between a lagoon and Grand Cul-de-Sac beach along the island's northeastern shore, the hotel is an education in understated elegance. Rooms are spare and enormous, with lots of wood and one or two pops of bright color—some even have small, rectangular plunge pools for mini-laps. The food at  Amis St. Barth is unabashedly modern French, with attention paid to proper portions in the tropics: in other words, not too much. Water sports enthusiasts have an expanse of calm shallow waters for kayaking, kite-surfing, and snorkeling—a flotilla of a dozen sea turtles that survived the storms of 2017 remain in residence and are easily visible.

Those who knew and loved Le Carl Gustaf the first time around will have even more reason to fall for it now that the Barriere group has taken over. The hotelier company—known for reviving particularly beloved but withering properties—has made sure to keep the spirit of Le Carl chic and easy. The raw wood and petite terraces still make it feel like the beach house of a fabulous French friend, yet the hotel’s reimagined approach to the environment gives it a 21st-century edge. Paris design firm Gilles and Boissier gussied up the 21 rooms with creams, stone, and linen, as well as a profusion of palms separating various spaces with a curtain of greenery. Suites have been reconfigured to catch sea breezes, providing natural air conditioning. And a fleet of electric bikes brings guests down the hill upon which the hotel stands like a lookout, over the town and coastline, to nearby Shell Beach, the perfect place for a picnic prepared by the hotel’s staff that feels, appropriately simple and chic—much like Le Carl itself.

Romance is taken to a whole other level at this adults-only St. Lucia resort. With 36 plunge pool suites, butler service, and a personalized bar with only the top-shelf, this enclave was made for couples to relax and reconnect. While there's no shortage of places to lounge or splash around in on property, the resort also offers an array of excursions to explore the gorgeous corner of the Caribbean St. Lucia lays claim to. From rainforest nature walks with a fully packed picnic basket to adrenaline-pumping ATV tours, Serenity at Coconut Bay knows there's many ways to take in all the gorgeous scenery.

#6122. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6121. My Favorite Villa: A Storybook Trullo in Puglia With Six Bedrooms, a Private Chef, and Olive Grove Views

My best friend and I had an entire six-bedroom estate in Puglia, Italy, to ourselves for three nights in early November. We could have invited another 10 people, but there was something rather wonderful about having all that space for just the two of us. The region's whitewashed streets had emptied of their summer crowds, and the countryside around our home away from home was quiet enough that we felt no particular urgency to go anywhere.

I'd been looking forward to sleeping in a trullo, one of the traditional dry-stone houses with conical roofs that dot this part of southern Italy. At Trullo delle Dame, my bedroom sat directly beneath one of those cones, and every night, I fell asleep looking up at the curved stone ceiling. It felt like a storybook hideaway reimagined by someone with a very good eye for design. The soaking tub in my room didn't hurt either.

The original stone walls and domed ceilings have been preserved throughout the restored trulli, with sleek off-white furniture, stone walls, and traditional glazed ceramic or terra-cotta ornaments called pumi strewn about. The six bedrooms, including five en suite bedrooms and a primary suite, are spread out across the property. While I was there with my friend, I kept thinking about how well the house would work for a multigenerational family trip. There's enough space for everyone to retreat to their own rooms, and plenty of reasons to come back together over a chef-prepared meal, a card game in the seating area overlooking the countryside, or a dip in the saltwater infinity pool.

My favorite spot in the estate was the outdoor kitchen—specifically at the enormous round dining table, complete with a giant lazy Susan. One afternoon, we made orecchiette there, shaping the little ears of pasta by hand, flour up to our wrists, before sitting down to eat what we'd made. I could picture a dozen people around that table on a summer evening, passing plates of pasta and pouring each other another glass of wine (which the Mandarin Oriental team will stock the fridge with upon request).

Throughout the stay, our days fell into an easy routine. We'd walk through the olive groves in the mornings, read on the couch in the afternoons, and spend a few hours on the loungers by the pool. The water was unheated, so we were content to stay poolside in November. But I imagine it's where everyone ends up in July.

As tempting as it was to stay put, there was too much good food and wine in the surrounding countryside to spend all three days at the house. We drove the three miles into Cisternino for a meal at Taverna della Torre, and I'm still thinking about the gnocchi with white truffles. Another afternoon took us to Giovanni Aiello, an independent winery near Putignano, where we got to help make some of the bottle labels. The cellar is beautiful, and you can even have your tasting inside an old wine barrel. With the towns of Martina Franca and Ostuni also within easy driving distance, we could have happily spent a few more days eating our way around Puglia.

Some little bites, courtesy of the private chef

Of course, we hardly needed to leave the house to eat well. Each morning, our private chef laid out a breakfast spread of fresh yogurt, meats and cheeses, pies, pancakes, juices, and fruit, along with freshly brewed cappuccinos. There was enough food to feed considerably more than two people, though we did our best. In the evenings, he prepared multicourse dinners using local, seasonal produce. Of everything he made, my favorite was a fava bean purée with roasted peppers.

As two busy working moms, we quickly got used to the luxury of not having to think about what anyone would eat. Waking up to a breakfast feast and a creamy coffee, knowing someone else would deal with the dishes, was perhaps the hardest thing to give up at the end of the trip. (My family may need to lower their breakfast expectations for the foreseeable future.) And while we thoroughly enjoyed our few days off from mom duties, I could see how having a chef would make a family vacation feel much more like a vacation for the parents too. No grocery runs, no figuring out what to cook for 12 people, and no kitchen to clean up afterward.

The writer participating in a pasta-making class in the outdoor kitchen

The fruits of their labor: lots of orecchiette!

If we came back with our kids, I'd happily sign them up for a pizza-making session while we snuck off for a massage in the olive groves, all activities the brand offers to guests. The trees, which produce the estate's own olive oil, also make a rather lovely setting for a yoga class, which can also be arranged during the warmer months.

A few things worth knowing before booking: The private chef, food, and drinks are charged separately from the villa rental. You'll also want a car to explore the neighboring towns, although the concierge can arrange transfers. And if you're coming in November, as we did, check restaurant opening hours before heading out, since some places shorten their hours after the summer season. The unheated pool is also worth keeping in mind if you're traveling with children outside the warmer months.

On the morning we left, our chef packed us meat-and-cheese sandwiches for the road. After three days of elaborate breakfasts and multicourse dinners, those sandwiches somehow ranked among my favorite things he'd made. As we drove away, I thought about how I'd happily come back with a houseful of friends and family in summer—but I'd want the same bedroom under the cone.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6120. A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

Update: Due to weather conditions, Macy's has postponed the parade to Saturday, November 28, starting at 8:30 a.m. "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," the store said in a statement.

Santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern New Jersey. Sitting about 10 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan in Moonachie’s industrial park district, the 72,000-square-foot warehouse is home to Macy’s Parade Studio, where 60 designers, carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and other artisans chip away year-round to prepare for one morning a year: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

This year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition. Instead of the normal 50 to 60 inflatables, there will be nearly 100. The usual 500 new costumes will be upped to 1,000, while more than 11,000 volunteers will be a part of the milestone event.

A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940

It’s a massive endeavor for a tradition that started as a two-block-long procession of Central Park Zoo animals, a handful of bands, and Santa, all traveling six miles from Harlem to the department store’s flagship in Herald Square at 34th and Broadway in 1924 (it was suspended for three years during World War II from 1942 to 1944). The parade led to the unveiling of Macy’s window displays with puppets by marionette artist Tony Sarg to kick off the holiday—and retail—season.

“It started as a bunch of Macy's immigrant coworkers coming together to create a party like they had in their home countries,” Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production, tells me during a visit in late September. But soon, the animals were deemed to be “too scary” for children. Three years later, the balloons debuted, the work of Sarg, who he calls “one of the godfathers of puppetry” and “our Walt Disney.” His genius idea: flip marionettes upside down to become high-flying balloons on strings, creating the iconic tradition we know today.

Taking a peek at the concept art hanging inside the Macy's workshop

Wandering through the facility is like making your way through a pop culture fun house. A pair of Minions hang from the rafters, mingling with Pokémon’s Pikachu and Goofy, who is stuck in a wreath. A Planter’s Peanut Ferris wheel spins in the center, while models of the parade’s own famous characters, Tom Turkey, Blue Hippopotamus, and the fishy pair Rainbow and Greybow Trout, sit out to dry in front of shelves lined with paint buckets of every hue.

“This is like our own Hollywood lot,” Kennedy says. Indeed, there’s the distinct feel of a soundstage paired with the wildest arts and crafts studio you've ever seen, all together feeling like something out of Willy Wonka’s dreams. Before making its home here in 2011, the Parade Studio was located inside the old Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey, for decades.

Despite the holiday joy bursting from every seam, parade preparation is serious business. Every single element is handcrafted and hand-painted. "Generally it all starts with a napkin sketch,” Kennedy explains of the initial rough drawing. “It goes into full modeling in 3-D, and then engineering, where we have to figure out how to get this thing into the real world.”

But year after year, like the true elves of the holiday season they are, they pull it off—testing every float and balloon for any and every possible weather condition—so that on Thanksgiving morning, the 3.5 million lining the Manhattan route as well as the nearly 35 million watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at home (airing on NBC and Peacock from 8:30 a.m. to noon) can just sit back and revel in the delights of the season.

“What makes the parade so special is that it is an event that has been produced by colleagues since it began in 1924, and it continues to be Macy Studios colleagues' gift to New York City and gift to people who are tuning in around the country to watch on television,” Macy’s director of production operations Kathleen Wright tells Traveler.

Below, we peek behind the scenes of the Macy’s Parade Studio as the team prepares for the 100th parade, and how they plan to honor the traditions of the last century.

Some of the 3-D printed models that serve as the blueprints for the parade's iconic floats

The larger-than-life magic of the parade starts on the smallest scale. In the Studio’s 3-D print room, nearly a dozen machines hum away, creating miniature models—the first step in conceiving how to build each float. But that’s not the only tool used. Recently, engineers and sculptors have turned to augmented reality goggles, not just to picture the elements, but even wearing them while sculpting to make sure they get details right in a 3-D space.

The day I visit, the team is problem-solving on the new Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs float, which features three oversized dog puppets.

An array of the painted models inside the studio

“When floats come to life through some sort of animation is when it’s at its peak,” Kennedy says. While animatronics could provide the movements, they would lack the human touch. “With a puppet, I can look directly at you, give you a little show, and then pan to the next person. You get a lot more energy and excitement. There’s a long history of puppetry in the parade, so we made a concerted effort to include it.”

The team works through solutions for the best way to have a puppeteer lie below the float bed, controlling the motions from below while positioned with body pillows that still allow them to see the parade-goers through a scrim. They consider using delivery truck slats to increase the height of the float so the puppeteer can remain comfortable and still operate the puppet.

Mr. Peanut is the historic parade's oldest character.

In another section, another new float is going for a test spin. Planters’ Mr. Peanut Power Plant will celebrate the parade’s oldest character, with peanut-shaped confetti erupting through his top hat, as well as a rotating Ferris wheel showcasing his evolution from 1916, starting with the napkin sketch created by a 13-year-old boy from Virginia.

Also on the floor is a puppet of the original character Mr. Inspector, a stern-looking comic book character with a top hat and magnifying glass, who first appeared as a balloon in the 1929 parade. This version of the character was taken out of the archives and freshened up in order to be part of Macy’s own Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes float.

“Everything has to be refurbished,” Kennedy says. “These are New York City streets—it’s not like a perfect Narnia land. So they hit a bump, we have to work through it, or if it rains, we have to check for water damage.”

While the methods are precise, the methodology is all about creativity and resourcefulness. Case in point: While working on the Wednesday Addams float in 2024, Tim Burton himself asked for more decay and rot. So a sculptor modified his glue gun to spray spider webs around the entire float. “It’s a good example of how anything can become a tool,” he says of making fiction come to life.

But there are some strict restrictions. Floats have to fold up to the size of a standard city bus in order to fit through the Lincoln Tunnel into Manhattan. The massive convoy travels in two nights before Thanksgiving. Once settled, the team reassembles every piece, some using cranes, as every float gets its final touches before the big day.

Peeking inside the planning of the parade's Mickey Mouse float

Next, we step into the Balloon Studio, where again, everything starts with a 3-D model. After it’s approved, a larger form “white model,” roughly a few feet long, is generated (clay models were used in the past) and used to hand-draw lines that determine the shapes and sizes of each piece of balloon fabric that needs to be cut and how they’ll be melded together, much like sewing with a dress pattern.

Dangling from beams above is a display of white models of the past, with the monotone versions of Super Mario, Buzz Lightyear, Snoopy, and the Pillsbury Doughboy, among others. But today the focus is on the freshly-completed Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse, hanging from a little stand to mimic levitation. I count no less than nine pieces of fabric sketched out in pencil just for the nose—and about 18 for the front side of each ear.

Artisans stitch together all the massive textiles that go onto the floats.

At the next station, we see a pair of artisans doing seemingly mundane work stitching large swaths of fabric together with sewing machines. To a trained eye, though, the scene is actually chock full of proprietary Macy’s secrets. While rubber was used in the past, today the balloons are made of off-white secret material the makeup of which is closely guarded. The material is heat-sealed together using these Macy’s-designed machines with wheels that heat up to 410 degrees Fahrenheit. Then the material is painted using a formula that’s also—you guessed it—proprietary.

The secrets all come together as the completed balloons are first inflated indoors to make sure that the paint looks good and to check how it behaves with air. Some are inspected in the Studio while others that require more space are pumped up from the floor since it would float at the nearby Prudential Center. The balloons are inflated at various stages to ensure the air is filling up as intended.

The big test came on November 7, when they hosted the annual Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium to see how the balloons behave in outdoor conditions, as well as give city agencies the chance to approve everything.

Once that’s checked off, the night before the parade is the Balloon Inflation (which is open to the public; stay tuned for details here), when each character is blown up on the streets of the Upper West Side and prepped for its own turkey trot through Midtown. “They really are flying pieces of art,” Kennedy says.

A dress from the costume operations studio

While the floats and balloons may get the headlines, there would be no parade without the nearly 11,000 volunteers who help make the day happen, which is now 2.5-miles from the Upper West Side to Herald Square—and they all have to be dressed for the occasion. This year at least 1,500 more costumes are needed, but that doesn't intimidate costume director and associate producer Kimberly Montgomery, who’s been doing this for 27 years. “It’s gone so fast because it’s just been so darn fun,” she says of her tenure.

Costumes follow after the design of the float, with the larger backdrop serving as the source of wardrobe inspiration.

Every costume always begins in the same place. “We start with the design of the float and then riff off of that to tell a story with live people,” she explains. Just then, she catches a glimpse of a new design of a float with street signs and immediately starts brainstorming: “Maybe people on bikes will give it some texture and energy.” After all, she sees the floats as roving stages. "They're like mini Broadway shows.”

When the very first 1924 parade arrived at Macy’s, it was met by employees dressed as clowns—and this year there will be 1,000 clowns throughout the parade, just a portion of the costume packets that she’s been working all year to assemble. And it's not just with what they'll wear. The late November weather is a major consideration as well. Costume kits also include ear and hand warmers, “the first two areas to get cold,” she says. Most costumes are also made loose enough so that the paraders can layer up underneath.

There are roughly 3,500 costumes produced for the balloon handler brigade.

Balloon handlers get a different treatment. “Their costumes are a lot simpler because they have to pay attention to what they're doing,” she says. In fact, some balloons, like Buzz Lightyear, Sorcerer’s Mickey, and the Minion have nearly 100 people handling them. In total, about 3,500 of the costumes are for balloon handlers. “It’s serious business, so they get a coverall and a tabard that’s color coded with a picture of the character they’re holding.” She points out Toad the mushroom for Mario and an alien planet for Buzz Lightyear. And for the Minions, the team even has little cowboy hats.

Of course there are odes to the past in the costumes too. Some historic costumes have been pulled out of the archives, like an intricate Broadway-quality Mother Goose dress. Others have been given new interpretations, like the original character Harold, who debuted in 1945 as a clown, but had stints as a baseball player (as he was seen in Miracle on 34th Street), fireman, and policeman. For this centennial, there will be 100 Harolds—25 of each iteration—as inflatable costumes (balloons aren’t the only ones that are blown up here!).

Prepping for the big day begin bright and early at 4:30 a.m.

With all this prep, dressing thousands of people then operates like clockwork, as they arrive around 4:30 a.m. at ballrooms around town in their street clothes and exit transformed. For 2.5 hours, shuttles transport them all to the parade start line.

After all the pomp and circumstances are over, Montgomery turns to a new phase of the process: Laundry. “All of this goes in giant piles of whites, darks, and colors. We’ve got to get it laundered and put back in size order.”

And once everything is back in order, they start again on the following year’s parade. “No matter what holiday it is, we always have our finger on the pulse of Thanksgiving,” Wright says.

#6119. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”
