#6104. How to Spend Christmas in Paris

Strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper. The city shines brighter each year with thousands of lights illuminating its famous squares and landmarks like the Champs-Elysées, dubbed the “world’s most beautiful avenue.” Holiday cheer seeps into each of the 20 arrondissements, decorated with larger-than-life garlands, forests of bauble-strewn fir trees, sculptural light displays, and wooden chalets doling out vin chaud (mulled wine) and holiday specialties like foie gras—best spread on subtly sweet pain d’épices (gingerbread).

Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them. Fête the season in true French fashion with a movable feast dining and drinking at some of the city’s most iconic institutions, from Left Bank cafés where famous writers and artists once gathered to the Palace hotels huddled around Place de la Concorde and Place Vendôme. And when you’re ready to indulge in Paris’s renowned retail therapy, swing by one of the grand magasins (department stores), which rank among the best in the world for their holiday window displays—New York City included—executed with the same style and precision as a couturier. The city may not be blanketed in snow, but the holiday spirit is as strong here as on the slopes in the French Alps—and even has the cuisine and chalets to prove it. If you’re planning to spend Christmas in Paris, you’ll find plenty of ways to celebrate, but these nine are some of the best things to do and see during the holidays in the City of Light.

Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:

Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lindsey Tramuta.

This winter, Oscar winner Cate Blanchett will lead the lighting ceremony of the 2 million LED lights illuminating the Champs-Elysées, running all the way up to the Arc de Triomphe. Sparkling each evening from 5:00 pm to 1:00 am, the most iconic avenue in Paris and its 400 balloon glass garland-adorned trees are coordinating with another famous landmark—the Eiffel Tower—twinkling in unison on the hour. Every quarter of an hour, the Champs-Elysées will put on a light show set to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and on December 24 and 25, the avenue will glow in Christmas-themed green and red. As part of the New Year’s Eve countdown to midnight under the Arc de Triomphe, when a music-themed fireworks show will ring in 2027, the lights will shine in a tricolor blue, white and red display running down the avenue. Making a grand return after a decade-long pause, a Christmas market will run from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe with more than 200 stalls and an ice rink near the Pavillon Ledoyen.

Dining with a view takes on a whole new meaning as you settle in by the panoramic windows on Ducasse sur Seine, the sole electric boat cruising the river. The floating restaurant is as gastronomic an experience as anything on land thanks to Alain Ducasse, the namesake chef behind the modern Parisian cuisine who claims a record-setting number of coveted Michelin stars. With chef Jean-Philippe Berens and the team prepping everything fresh on board, you’ll have prime views of the Seine while dining in style on Christmas Eve during the six-course menu, which features everything from silky foie gras royale to raw scallops topped with gelée and caviar—plus a cheese course with 18-month-matured truffled Comté.

The ambiance is equally as elegant at Ducasse Baccarat, where the chef’s cuisine is presented in an opulent space dripping in chandeliers and tableware designed by the French fine crystal creator. One of the few spots open daily during the holiday season, the restaurant ups the ante on Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve with themed degustation menus.

France’s Capital of Christmas, Strasbourg, is home to the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but Paris is dotted with more than a dozen markets and Christmas villages—the largest being La Magie de Noël in the Tuileries Garden, stretching from the Louvre to Place de la Concorde, which remains open until early January. There, you’ll discover hundreds of wooden cabins selling small gifts and seasonal treats; a selection of stands run by French artisans, from glassblowers to woodworkers; and attractions like a small ice rink and carnival rides—the Ferris wheel being the highlight, especially during the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show.

On the Square René Viviani, directly across from Notre Dame, you’ll find an intimate market with some 30 exhibitors selling regional food, hot chocolate, and handmade crafts. On the Left Bank, the Saint-Germain-des-Prés Marché de Noël unfolds along the namesake boulevard, next to the church, with wooden chalets and gourmet stands serving up everything from caviar and foie gras to Savoyard favorite tartiflette (a reblochon cheese and potato gratin) and sweet and savory pretzels. Unfolding in the courtyard of the Gare de l’Est train station, the historic starting point for the first Orient Express, the Marché de Noël des Producteurs Alsaciens is dedicated to Alsatian delicacies, with stands displaying regional specialties like kougelhopf, a fluted brioche cake filled with rum-soaked raisins and almonds.

More than the decorated avenues and elaborate window displays, it is the Bûche de Noël (yule log cakes that may or may not be shaped like logs) that takes the lead as the ultimate holiday essential during Christmas in Paris. While most cakes are prepared and sold for take-away, there are a few spots to linger over tea and an individual slice of the indulgent Christmas cake, including Fouquet’s Paris, where the red, velvety chocolate and roasted corn mousse dessert is designed after the arabesques in the hotel’s historic salons and staircases. At Butterfly Pâtisserie, the Hôtel de Crillon’s boutique and tearoom, pastry chef Matthieu Carlin’s exquisite selection of seasonal pastries, including his Bolivian dark chocolate mousse Bûche de Noël, shaped like a submarine out of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea—a tribute to the hotel’s Jules Verne-inspired holiday theme—can be enjoyed on-site with a cup of tea or a thick hot chocolate, or taken to-go. On the Place de la Concorde, snack on praline hazelnut and pistachio and orange blossom-flavored French toast from the hotel’s garland-strewn, striped winter chalet, or sip espresso martinis at Terrasse Concorde’s pop-up bar, which has been redecorated to mimic the most exclusive of ski resorts with French cashmere house Kujten’s custom-crafted cushions and blankets.

At Ritz Paris, craft your own yule log during a baking class, or settle in by the fireplace of the opulent, champagne-colored Salon Marie-Louise for a Christmas tea, where you’ll indulge in spruced-up takes on the afternoon tradition, including truffle cream finger sandwiches, lobster focaccia, and Crêpes Suzettes prepped à la minute. Next door, Ritz Paris Le Comptoir’s carousel-shaped Bûche de Noël has been deemed the city’s most stunning this season—and with only 65 available, it’s a gift unlike any other. Nearby at Mondovi Luxury Suites, chefs come to you for in-suite macaron-making sessions and mixology workshops—and with the “world’s best bartender” Colin Field behind the Le 7 Cocktail Bar, you’ll be learning from the best. On the Left Bank, the palace hotel Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris is serving a lavish Sunday brunch buffet, winter-themed afternoon tea with hot chocolate, and pastry chef Nicolas Guercio’s wreath-shaped yule log filled with layers of vanilla mousse, pear confit, and housemade pecan praline.

Dating back to the mid-13th century, Sainte-Chapelle was once a royal chapel constructed to house the precious Crown of Thorns relic. Today, it’s admired for a different reason: the 15 stained-glass windows—comprised of 1,113 panels—are some of the most impressive in France, let alone all of Europe. Combine sightseeing with an experience only taking place during the holiday season listening to the music of Antonio Vivaldi or Johann Strauss during a classical concert within the chapel’s Gothic nave.

Paris’s grand magasins (department stores) offer more than retail therapy. Their elaborate holiday window displays executed in couture-like fashion have earned them the title of best in the world—and that even includes New York City. There’s a theme for every taste: The Samaritaine has been designed to feel like you’re taking a Christmas stroll through a snowy Paris, with winter lights and snowflakes crowning the grand magasin’s facade near the Seine. Shop at the indoor Christmas market and rest assured your presents will sit pretty under the tree this year thanks to the help of the pros at the dedicated wrapping studio, who can swath gifts in plush paper and custom-made ribbons. Over at Printemps Haussmann, behind the Opéra Garnier, the department store decorated its windows around the theme of “A Well-Knit Christmas," commissioning artisan-crafted crochet pieces; 160 animated characters (including felt cats and mice) chasing a ball of wool; and costumes by the store’s seamstress, Valérie Cuter.

At Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, holiday cheer doesn't end at the sidewalk, where French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac themed the vibrant window displays around tales of angels and Matisse-inspired shapes. The Christmas tree and holiday displays beneath the store's Art Nouveau dome are an annual event, comparable to New York City’s Rockefeller Center tree lighting. Always vibrant and impressive, visitors who venture into the atrium of the shop this season will find a tree towering 16 meters high—but this year, the wing-shaped structure follows the animated storybook theme with an angel hovering overhead and a soundtrack by French DJ Vladimir Cauchemar. From the 30-foot-long Glasswalk footbridge, on the third floor of the store, you can catch an even better view of the “tree”—and snap a few photos. Hotels like SO/ Paris, on the banks of the Seine, are also dressing up for the occasion with paper artist Maud Vantours’ sculptural Nutcracker creation, which you can admire while sipping seasonal coffee or an espresso martini along with a slice of the hotel’s Bûche de Noël.

Nothing warms up locals and visitors like hot chocolate. For the most well-known, head to Angelina on the rue de Rivoli for its thick, decadent Chocolat Chaud Africain that will leave you wondering if they just melted an entire chocolate bar into your cup. If the line snakes around the block, take it à emporter. Near the Opéra Garnier, chocolatier Jade Genin (daughter of legendary Jacques Genin) is famous for her signature Concorde obelisk-shaped chocolate pyramidions, but her modernized take on hot chocolate—entirely plant-based with homemade almond milk—is as much a draw during the holidays. In Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Les Deux Magots’s scarlet banquettes may have been where the literary set like Jean-Paul Sartre once held court, but the cafe is also one of the best on the Left Bank for hot chocolate—where it’s prepared the traditional way, with melted Valrhona blended with warm milk and poured out of a classic carafe.

While you can spike your hot chocolate with Irish whiskey and Chantilly cream, the city’s leading cocktail bars are taking some of the holiday season’s signature flavors and mixing them into creations like Beurre, Little Red Door’s cocktail version of fresh brioche, with crisp apple, butter, vodka, and yes—bread. At The Cambridge Public House, classic Irish coffee is given a French twist with calvados and silky salted maple cream, while Hôtel Lancaster partnered with historic French tea house Damman Frères for a gingerbread punch blended with rooibos de Noël tea and sherry, served alongside a tonka bean and gingerbread pastry.

Moulin Rouge’s lavish costumes adorned with sequins and rhinestones feel all the more festive when you’re dressed up yourself on Christmas night for a gourmet feast followed by the iconic Féerie revue show. At the Musée des Arts Forains (Fairground Museum), its annual Christmas extravaganza, Le Festival du Merveilleux, runs from December 26, 2026, to January 3, 2027. The makeshift Christmas village transforms into a light-strewn theater with magicians, aerial silk dancers, musicians, puppeteers, and tap dancers putting on dreamlike performances around the Belle Époque funfairs and gardens.

On Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, get your culture fix while sightseeing, sipping champagne, and listening to an orchestra perform carols and violin concertos during a classical Christmas show in one of the world’s most famous landmarks: the Eiffel Tower. And for the full winter wonderland experience, Disneyland Park’s characters are adorned in holiday attire during Christmas parades, musical performances by The Arendelle Carollers in the new World of Frozen, and meet-and-greet moments with Santa hat-clad favorites like Stitch.

Embrace the festive feel of slope-side specialties like fondue at Chalet des Îles, a historic wooden Swiss chalet reconstructed by Napoleon III for Eugénie that hovers on an island in the Bois de Boulogne. Top Chef contestant and co-founder of Paris’s Ambos restaurant, Pierre Chomet, is behind this season’s fireside feast of Alsatian-style tartes, flambées, and creamy Mont d’Or cheese, while Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme’s timber-clad Chalet du Park has popped up for the season in the Palace hotel’s terrace, serving winter menus designed by Michelin-starred chef Jean-François Rouquette.

At Hôtel Le Grand Mazarin, join a chocolate expert for small-group tastings, or take a seat for Christmas Eve dinner at candlelit restaurant Boubalé for a Mediterranean take on traditional plates like toasted challah with foie gras and fig and scallops wrapped in kadaif (shredded phyllo) paired with a holiday-themed DJ set. A dinner worth dressing up for, two Michelin-starred Le Clarence, off of the Champs-Elysées, has designed a feast worthy of royalty complete with the finest of ingredients, from dive-caught scallops to lobster and caviar—plus a collector-worthy wine pairing that fêtes the season in true French fashion.

#6103. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6102. Avianca Adds New U.S. Route

Colombian flag carrier Avianca is adding a new connection to the U.S. Northeast.

Starting Feb. 2, 2027, the airline will offer service between Barranquilla and New York-JFK.

Flights will operate four times weekly using Airbus A320-family aircraft, each with up to 180 seats.

“The launch of this nonstop route to New York reaffirms our commitment to [Barranquilla] and the entire Colombian Caribbean region,” Avianca President Gabriel Oliva said in a statement. “We want to continue connecting regions with major international markets, making travel easier, supporting tourism, and contributing to Colombia’s economic development.”

Avianca currently serves JFK from Bogota, Cartagena, Medellín, Pereira, Colombia, Guatemala City, San Salvador, El Salvador, Quito, and Guayaquil. From Barranquilla, it flies to Miami, Bogota, Medellín, and Cali.

#6101. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6100. How JetBlue's Bag Fee Hike Makes A BlueFirst Base Fare From $249, Bag Included, Look Like A Real Alternative

Changes are happening at JetBlue Airways. The airline recently raised its bag fees for economy passengers; as of November 3, the first checked bag will cost between $50 and $70, depending on the day and when the ticket is booked, while a second checked bag ranges from $70 to $85. These are steep prices and noticeably higher than the checked bag fees set by US legacy carriers, while JetBlue's base fares before optional add-ons tend to be lower than the competition.

At the same time, JetBlue will soon introduce 'BlueFirst', a domestic first class cabin that will be rolled out fleetwide. The carrier will debut this cabin on December 8 on its route from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, before introducing the cabin throughout its network. While JetBlue prices all fares dynamically, BlueFirst one-way fares will start at $249 when the cabin is first introduced, and while this certainly doesn't mean all tickets will be priced this way, those that are will be very compelling compared with the airline's economy cabin.

JetBlue offers three fare types for its Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint cabin classes: Base, Standard, and Flex. None of the fares for Main and EvenMore include checked bags, meaning passengers who want to check their bags need to add at least $50 to the overall price of their tickets. At the same time, the airline's new BlueFirst fares do include at least one checked bag, while the BlueFirst Flex fare includes two checked bags. What makes this particularly notable is that BlueFirst fares are actually fairly attractive.

The airline's one-way BlueFirst fares start at $299 from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, and the route between LaGuardia and Fort Lauderdale follows shortly afterward, with prices starting at $249. Although most tickets are being sold for significantly more, the airline has largely priced BlueFirst fares at about 40% to 70% more than an equivalent Main ticket.

Crucially, however, even the BlueFirst Base ticket includes a checked bag, slightly closing the gap. The BlueFirst Flex includes two checked bags, whereas a Main Flex or an EvenMore Flex fare includes none. While the full cost of a BlueFirst ticket will still be higher, it's closer than expected.

With the recent increase in bag fees, BlueFirst tickets do look quite attractive for passengers who will check a bag and are willing to pay more for a better experience. BlueFirst offers a large recliner with added legroom, as well as complimentary meals and premium drinks. It undoubtedly offers a more comfortable experience than Main, and the price difference is not particularly steep once ancillaries are factored. What's more, JetBlue's initial pricing for BlueFirst does not follow the standard practice in the US.

Generally, the US legacy carriers (which are the airlines that have offered domestic first class the longest) do not price first class tickets at 40% to 70% above economy. Domestic first class fares are usually significantly more expensive than economy tickets, and even when you factor in ancillaries, first class comes at a real price premium. Admittedly, JetBlue's initial BlueFirst tickets are being sold in the competitive Florida market, where fares tend to be low, but they still largely undercut the legacy carriers on price.

One way to view this is as a deliberate strategy by JetBlue. The airline has never before offered a domestic first class cabin, and it plans to introduce BlueFirst throughout the network fairly rapidly. Not only do potential customers need to be made aware of the product and exposed to it, but the carrier also needs to pull customers away from American, Delta, and United. Attractive initial fares help with publicity while increasing bookings, which heightens awareness.

On the flip side, however, airlines generally charge what they think is the maximum price that customers are willing to pay. JetBlue undercutting competitors on price can also be seen as a reflection of the carrier's pricing power, which isn't a positive sign. One reason JetBlue introduced BlueFirst was to increase revenue, since first class generally commands higher fares. If it continues to undercut competitors on price system-wide, then this would become a problem.

The aircraft has become a tool the airline desperately needs during a period of financial struggle.

JetBlue operates like a budget airline, such as Frontier or Allegiant Air. However, the airline has differentiated itself not necessarily through low fares, but through the passenger experience. The carrier offered significantly more legroom in economy, along with seatback screens before they became common on domestic flights. In addition, snack options were diverse, and the airline's later Mint business class on transcontinental and transatlantic routes has been well received.

Despite its low-cost carrier structure, the airline offers a passenger experience similar to that of legacy carriers, and arguably better in some ways. However, JetBlue has been unable to command a fare premium for its excellent economy product, while its Northeast operations come with high operating costs. In addition, the airline didn't offer first class in the past, further limiting revenue, and the carrier has faced serious challenges expanding its customer base.

Fort Lauderdale Hollywood International Airport (FLL)

New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK)

San Juan Luis Munoz Marin International Airport (SJU)

While JetBlue is an attractive option for customers in the Northeast, its route network is quite minimal outside of the East Coast. Its network and schedules are not attractive to much of the country. In addition, JetBlue has also suffered major reliability challenges. This hurts its appeal to many potential customers, as operational reliability is a major factor in purchasing decisions. While BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's issues, it should help the carrier with its network-wide revenue problem.

Not only do premium seats such as domestic first class have superior margins to economy seats, but premium demand is through the roof in the US. By not offering a domestic first-class product until now, JetBlue has essentially lost out on lucrative revenue, and several other low-cost carriers are now offering such a product. Frontier and Allegiant Air have both revealed domestic first class cabins to debut in 2027, while Breeze Airways already sells first class seats.

Notably, JetBlue will largely maintain the same capacity its planes currently have. It will achieve this by cutting seat pitch in Main down to just 30 inches (76.2 centimeters), even though the airline has long been known for offering above-average seat pitch. While this is undoubtedly a drawback for most customers, JetBlue hasn't been able to command a fare premium for offering more legroom. Therefore, it will focus on where the money is, which is in the new BlueFirst cabin, while it will also make its cabins more space-efficient.

Of course, BlueFirst won't solve all of JetBlue's issues; the airline has limited national relevance, and on-time operations remain challenging. What's more, JetBlue's overall financial situation has deteriorated significantly over the past several years. However, the new BlueFirst cabin should help the airline's revenue stream and also make the airline more appealing to potential customers, who may have stayed away from the airline due to the lack of a domestic first class cabin.

JetBlue’s BlueFirst cabin is nearing its launch after FAA certification cleared a key regulatory hurdle.

For travelers living in New York, Boston, Florida, or San Juan, JetBlue offers fairly comprehensive schedules and good route options. However, airlines such as Delta Air Lines and United Airlines operate routes that span the entire country, making them relevant nationally. In addition, these airlines have long offered domestic first class, which is a major reason to be loyal to one airline. What's more, JetBlue's operational reliability issues make customers more hesitant to choose it over other airlines.

The airline has not made money since 2019 and has posted a $257 million loss for the third quarter of 2026. The carrier has attractive assets, including a large slot portfolio at New York JFK Airport, and is generally liked by its loyal customers. However, the route network loses money, and frequent-flyer engagement is not high enough to offset these losses (legacy carriers make most of their money through co-branded credit card engagement rather than ticket sales).

The carrier has been implementing the 'JetForward' turnaround plan to cut unprofitable routes, improve operational reliability, and refocus on leisure customers. BlueFirst is one of the most consequential decisions the airline has made in recent years, and it should significantly improve the carrier's revenue stream given strong demand for premium cabins today. What remains to be seen is whether the JetForward initiative and moves such as introducing BlueFirst will be enough to ensure the airline's long-term survival.

#6099. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6098. United Airlines Pilot Suspended On TSA Orders Over Support For Terror Group, Report Says

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has reportedly directed United Airlines to suspend a pilot last week over alleged support for a terrorist organization. According to a report by Jewish News Syndicate (JNS), citing a federal government source, the pilot's crew security credential was also revoked. Neither the pilot's identity nor the terrorist organization they allegedly supported has been disclosed.

The reported intervention follows several controversies surrounding United pilots and comes amid heightened international scrutiny of aviation personnel following an attempted terrorist attack aboard a flydubai flight in September. CNN reports that US security agencies have subsequently issued a joint advisory to the aviation industry warning of renewed calls for attacks against commercial aviation.

The federal intervention reportedly occurred between November 16 and 22, and included the withdrawal of the pilot's Known Crewmember (KCM) credential, which facilitates expedited security screening for eligible airline employees. The existing program is already undergoing significant changes, with the Association of Flight Attendants confirming that its replacement, the Crewmember Access Point (CMAP) program, will be administered directly by the TSA by the end of 2026.

The suspension follows earlier reporting by journalist Mike Wagenheim on November 17, citing two sources who alleged that United was aware of up to six additional crew members who had expressed support for terrorist organizations. According to View From The Wing, the federal source subsequently alleged that resistance from the pilots' union contributed to the TSA's decision to intervene.

JNS approached both United and the TSA for comment on multiple occasions, but was not able to obtain a response from either organization. However, Michael Wilson, spokesperson for United's Master Executive Council of the Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), explained that the union assesses allegations against its professional ethics code and United's workplace guidelines, stating that:

“[The union] has a robust professional standards committee and legal team that evaluates any accusation or pilot action.”

The latest case follows renewed scrutiny of United Captain Ibrahim Mossallam, a Newark-based pilot qualified to operate the Boeing 757 and 767. United initially suspended Mossallam with pay in November 2023 after he published social media comments praising the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on Israel. According to Airline Ratings, he subsequently returned to flying duties, although Aerotime reported last month that United had confirmed that he had again been removed from service pending a review.

A separate controversy emerged in October when the Jerusalem Post reported that Israeli authorities had barred United pilot Sina Amjadian from operating flights into the country following allegations of support for Hezbollah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, United responded that Amjadian, a Boeing 737 pilot, was not qualified on United's long-haul aircraft, and had been on leave since 2024.

Mossallam publishes controversial comments concerning the October 7 attacks.

Mossallam reportedly returns to flying duties.

United confirms Mossallam has again been withheld from service.

United denies reports of Mossallam's immediate reinstatement.

Israel's restrictions on Amjadian become public.

Allegations emerge concerning six additional crew members.

TSA reportedly orders the suspension of an unnamed pilot.

Details of the reported TSA intervention are published.

While United has confirmed the employment status of both previously identified pilots, several other allegations remain unverified. The carrier has also explicitly denied reports that Mossallam returned to flying immediately after his latest suspension. Nevertheless, the reported intervention by federal authorities raises important questions about where an airline's responsibility for assessing potential security threats ends, and the government's begins.

It has also emerged that some of the pilot's colleagues gave up first class seats to monitor him on a flight he was operating.

The potential consequences of insider threats were demonstrated on September 30, when a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv became the subject of an attempted terrorist attack involving its first officer. The aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia, and the UAE's attorney general subsequently characterized the incident as an attempted suicide attack.

In the US, the TSA's authority extends considerably beyond airport security checkpoints. Under Section 46111 of Title 49 of the US Code, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) must take action when notified by the TSA of a qualifying security threat. The TSA can also request that the action take immediate effect and, separately, issue mandatory security directives to airlines.

Removes expedited crew access privileges.

Requires airlines to implement specified security measures.

Temporarily removes relevant flying privileges.

Removes privileges conferred by the certificate.

Although there is no evidence that the United pilots were planning similar attacks, the broader security threat remains real. On November 19, the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and TSA jointly warned US airlines and airports about extremist calls for further attacks following the flydubai incident. While authorities were reportedly unaware of any specific credible plot, the advisory underscores the importance of preventative security measures, rigorous personnel vetting, and federal intervention powers.

#6097. ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects New Council Members

Edited By: Vanni Gibertini

Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.

Over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

“Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the Conference.

Participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked States, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

The Conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Plan. It also supported liberalizing air services agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since new air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing States. ICAO’s statement continued: “The Conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”

Participants were asked to express their views on the documentation proposing various initiatives with regards to consumer protection legislations that have become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

At the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop Core Principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:

The report for the Seventh Conference invites States to modernize their consumer-protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also says legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries and other providers regarding information, complaints and disruption assistance.

ICAO is expected to review its Core Principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

Many Member States cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

The Conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”

The rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic Member States will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while States will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

During the final two days of the Conference, ICAO held an Extraordinary Session of its Assembly to elect the four additional Council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The Council is the Organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the Assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

Six candidates competed for the four new seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand and Türkiye. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four States won seats.

The Council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uruguay.

The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

#6096. Why A Part 103 Ultralight Needs No Pilot's License In The US & Weighs Under 254 Pounds

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

Many people assume that flying any type of aircraft requires extensive training, a pilot certificate, medical approval, and federal registration. While that holds true for most types of licenses, such as a Certified Flight Instructor certificate (CFI) or Airline Transport Pilot (ATP), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has long maintained a narrow exception that allows certain recreational flyers to take to the skies without obtaining a pilot license. The exception falls under FAA Part 103, a section of federal regulations governing ultralight vehicles and the strict limitations placed upon them.

While Part 103 is broadly described as allowing someone to fly without a license, the reality is more nuanced. The regulation applies only to a highly specific category of lightweight recreational aircraft that must meet strict performance, weight, and operating requirements. Understanding what qualifies under Part 103 helps explain where the FAA draws the line between recreational freedom and traditional pilot certification requirements.

Yes, you can legally fly an aircraft in the United States without a pilot certificate, but only if the aircraft qualifies as an ultralight vehicle under FAA Part 103. These vehicles occupy a unique regulatory category that exempts operators from requirements including pilot licensing, aircraft registration, airworthiness certification, and medical certification. The exemption was created to support recreational flying while limiting risk through strict aircraft performance restrictions.

For powered ultralights, the FAA limits empty weight to 254 lb (115.2 kg), fuel capacity to five gallons (18.9 liters), maximum level-flight speed to 55 knots, and maximum power-off stall speed to 24 knots. Because these aircraft are intentionally small and limited in capability, the FAA regulates them differently than conventional airplanes.

The concept dates back decades, when regulators sought a framework that would allow simple recreational flying without imposing the full regulatory burden associated with general aviation aircraft. Rather than focusing on pilot certification, Part 103 controls risk by limiting what the aircraft can do. According to the FAA's regulations, qualifying ultralight vehicles are intended solely for sport and recreational purposes and are limited to carrying a single occupant.

A common misconception is that any small aircraft can be flown without a license. In reality, FAA Part 103 sets detailed technical requirements an aircraft must meet to qualify as an ultralight vehicle. The term Ultralight is a specific category issued by the FAA for licensing and certification, such as airplane, rotorcraft, or glider for pilot ratings. While an FAA certificate typically prints the category and class, the lack of a true license requirement omits this display.

The most important requirements involve weight, occupancy, fuel capacity, and performance. Powered Ultralights operate on the basis of minimal configurations of these variables. Ultralight aircraft should not be confused with Light Sport Aircraft, the next category up in the FAA's classification; they also have slightly different regulatory requirements, such as a higher speed limit of 250 knots and the ability to carry an additional passenger. These privileges come at the cost of training for a sport pilot certificate, among other requirements as outlined in 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart J, and 14 CFR Part 91.327.

Unpowered ultralights, such as many hang gliders, fall under a different weight limit. Under Part 103, these vehicles must weigh less than 155 pounds (70.3 kg) empty. By restricting both weight and performance, the FAA effectively prevents Part 103 aircraft from evolving into conventional airplanes that would normally require certification and pilot qualification.

Discover the two paths to becoming a commercial pilot and which one might be right for you.

Although operators are exempt from licensing requirements, they are not exempt from federal aviation regulations. FAA Part 103 establishes operational limitations designed to protect both ultralight pilots and the public on the ground. Interestingly enough, Ultralight aircraft are not governed by either 14 CFR Part 61 or Part 91, which is the usual home for general aviation operation guidelines.

Among the most important restrictions are where and when ultralights may fly. Operations are generally limited to daylight hours and must avoid congested areas, cities, towns, and open-air assemblies of people. The rules also restrict operations within controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, E, and most special use airspace) unless prior authorization has been obtained from air traffic control.

These requirements show that the FAA's approach is not deregulation but targeted regulation. Operators may not need a pilot certificate, but they are still responsible for understanding airspace, weather conditions, and applicable operating restrictions before every flight. For many ultralight enthusiasts, voluntary training remains a common safety practice despite the absence of a licensing requirement.

While FAA regulations do not require formal flight training for Part 103 operations, aviation organizations consistently encourage it. Groups such as the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) have long promoted structured training programs for ultralight pilots, emphasizing that regulatory exemptions do not eliminate the risks associated with flight.

The EAA's Ultralight Sourcebook notes that Part 103 provides significant operational freedom but also places responsibility squarely on the operator. Similarly, many flight instructors and aviation educators recommend dual instruction in two-seat trainers before attempting solo ultralight operations. Pilot Institute has also highlighted that, despite the absence of licensing requirements, knowledge of weather, aerodynamics, and operating limitations remains critical for safe flight. Industry recommendations reflect a broader understanding that flying skills and regulatory requirements are not necessarily the same thing. A pilot may legally operate a Part 103 vehicle without a certificate, but aviation organizations generally view training as one of the most effective safety measures available.

Cost is another important variable. While flight training for a Private Pilot License (PPL) can range from $9,000 to $130,000, Ultralight aircraft operation has a less burdensome barrier to entry. Because no official license is required by the FAA, training costs alone are significantly lower. In general, however, ultralight aircraft are much less common in the general aviation landscape than, for instance, a Cessna 172. The good news is that outright ownership of ultralight aircraft is also more accessible. Aerocorner reports that the cheapest new ultralight aircraft in 2026 is the Mini-Max 1103R, a single-seat wood-and-fabric kit that Mini-Max USA lists at $10,899.99 for the airframe. Also available is a finished, ready-to-fly example at about $22,500.

Ultralight aircraft are simplified, open-air flying machines for recreation, not requiring the same government approval as standard airplanes.

The same restrictions that make Part 103 accessible can also limit its practicality. Ultralight aircraft operation is the strictest modality of aviation under the FAA's jurisdiction. While the qualifications are generally among the most accessible to the public, that accessibility comes with significant compromises. Aircraft designed to remain under the FAA's weight and performance limits generally offer less range, lower speed, and reduced capability compared to certified airplanes.

Weather sensitivity is another consideration. Because ultralights are lightweight and often have minimal protection from the elements, operating conditions that might be manageable for larger aircraft can present greater challenges. The single-seat requirement also prevents pilots from carrying passengers or instructors during normal operations. Under Part 103, ultralight vehicles must fly during daytime hours with visual reference to the surface and meet basic Visual Flight Rules (VFR) weather minimums for their prescribed airspace. Reference to published manufacturer minimums is also imperative, particularly with respect to wind.

Prospective ultralight pilots should also remember that local airspace considerations still matter. Before operating any Part 103 vehicle, operators should ensure they understand applicable airspace restrictions and any authorization requirements that may apply near busy airports. In the United States, ultralight aircraft cannot fly over congested areas or crowds, and they cannot enter controlled airspace (Class A, B, C, D, or surface Class E) without prior Air Traffic Control (ATC) authorization. Advisory Circular AC-91-36D also suggests that ultralight pilots voluntarily remain above 2000 feet (609.6 meters) above ground level (AGL) wherever possible.

The short answer is yes: FAA Part 103 allows certain ultralight vehicles to be flown legally in the United States without a pilot certificate, aircraft registration, medical certification, or airworthiness approval. However, that freedom exists only because the FAA imposes strict restrictions on aircraft weight, speed, fuel capacity, occupancy, and operating conditions.

Rather than creating a loophole in aviation regulation, Part 103 represents a carefully structured compromise. The FAA permits recreational flyers to avoid many traditional certification requirements while ensuring that the aircraft themselves remain limited in capability and risk exposure.

For aviation enthusiasts, Part 103 continues to provide one of the most accessible entry points into personal flight. Yet the regulation's enduring message remains clear: while a license may not be required, safe operation still depends on knowledge, preparation, and respect for the limitations of both the aircraft and the environment in which it flies.

#6095. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6094. Qantas Launches 5 New Nonstop Routes For 2027: See Full List Now

Qantas is currently set to launch five new routes between January and October 2027. They include a new link announced on November 26, when this article was written, which will be operated by QantasLink. Of course, compared to some of the other entries, it might not seem particularly noteworthy, but it is in its own right.

As the article only focuses on 2027, the upcoming link from Sydney to Las Vegas, which will begin on December 29, is not included. Qantas will serve this market six times weekly using the Boeing 787-9. It'll be the first time that scheduled flights have existed, although charter services operated in the past.

Obviously, a lot of the attention is on the much-discussed nonstop service from Sydney to London Heathrow, which will deploy the Airbus A350-1000ULR. The maximum block time is expected to be around 21 hours.

Reflecting the highly prestigious nature of the route, AeroRoutes shows that it'll use QF1/QF2, which is currently on Qantas' one-stop operation from Sydney to Heathrow via Singapore. The stopping service will then use QF5/QF6. Those numbers are currently on Sydney-Perth-Rome, which will become QF105/QF106.

3 weekly QantasLink Dash 8-Q400 (Sunstate). See the next section

4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates

4 weekly QantasLink E190 (Alliance). Jetstar also operates

3 weekly 787-9. Qantas will now have 3 routes to South Africa. It'll be Cape Town's longest nonstop service in the Southern Hemisphere

The so-called Project Sunrise, and everything related to it, has been discussed in detail on many occasions. Tickets are meant to go on sale in February

Theoretically, the nonstop operation to Heathrow will cover 9,100+ nautical miles (16,853+ km) each way. However, this is before adjusting the distance because of detours for closed airspace and chasing tailwinds and lower airspace costs. It'll cover more distance than that. Still, even before the alteration, it'd exceed the length of what is currently number one, Singapore Airlines to New York JFK, by around 11%.

Questions might be raised about the appeal of the upcoming nonstop service from Albury to the popular Gold Coast, which will have a maximum block time of two hours and 20 minutes on the Q400. However, QantasLink will be the third airline to attempt it since 2017.

Cirium Diio data shows that the now-defunct JetGo flew in 2017/2018 using the Embraer ERJ135 and ERJ140. The now-defunct carrier Bonza followed in 2023/2024 using the Boeing 737 MAX 8. Bonza primarily focused on unserved markets, whether without head-to-head competition or brand-new.

Like low-cost carriers elsewhere, Bonza used its higher-capacity equipment with much lower seat-mile costs to offer much more attractive fares, compounded by flying nonstop rather than connecting on the way. The lower fares were entirely to drive demand and therefore to grow the market's traffic.

Booking data shows that Albury-Gold Coast passengers increased by nearly 400% to over 23,000 in a year after the airline's entry. Of course, demand stimulation from the lower fares depressed the yields, but that always happens with LCCs. It is unclear if Bonza's fares fell by more or less than the traffic growth. It is unknown what the average fare was to achieve an approximate 80% load factor.

QantasLink's operation will be radically different. It'll deploy the 76-seat Q400 rather than the 189-seat MAX 8, reducing round-trip weekly seats for sale from 1,134 to just 456. It'll not have to discount anywhere near as dramatically. That's just as well, as its much higher costs wouldn't let it, at least not sustainably. That's why its minimum round-trip fare is about USD$344 (AU$518). By only flying at more popular times of the year, rather than for weeks at a time and having to discount more, yields will not be depressed.

Both of these places stopped seeing the carrier in 2026, but things could be changing...

QantasLink's new route to the Gold Coast will cover 579 nautical miles (1,072 km) each way. However, if statute miles are used instead, it'll be 666 miles, the so-called number of the beast. Schedule analysis suggests that only 11 routes globally will have this great circle distance when the Q400 service lifts off in March.

It will be Albury's second-longest turboprop-driven scheduled link in nearly three years. QantasLink had operated the Q400 to Brisbane between July 2021 and May 2024, but that route has switched to the 96-seat E190 (other capacities operate occasionally). More seats contributed to the route's frequency falling to daily, down from the record high of two daily flights with the Q400.
